title: Optimal Four-copy Detection Of The Three-tangle And Its Fault-tolerant Cost
authors: Federico Tom\'as B. P\'erez, Berta Casas, I-Chi Chen, Su Yeon Chang, Philipp Schleich, M. Cerezo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The three-tangle, [MATH], is a measure of genuine tripartite entanglement that distinguishes GHZ-type from W-type entanglement in pure three-qubit states. Here, we identify the statistically optimal one-sided four-copy detector of the three-tangle and study its implementation cost. The optimal detector has click probability [MATH], while previous four-copy constructions achieve [MATH] and therefore require asymptotically [MATH] times as many experimental repetitions. Using the representation-theoretic structure of the problem, we construct an ancilla-free implementation of the optimal detector using 15 CNOT gates, together with an 11-CNOT detector with click probability [MATH]. These results reveal a tradeoff between statistical efficiency and implementation cost, since reducing the number of repetitions requires increasingly expensive circuits. We then show that this tradeoff persists once the circuits are encoded. In a fully fault-tolerant setting, the increased click probability comes with a substantial non-Clifford synthesis cost, while an early fault-tolerant implementation based on [MATH] gates and STAR rotations reduces this overhead at the expense of additional encoded resources. We quantify these costs using both the Steane and [MATH] codes, providing explicit resource estimates for implementing the optimal detector across different computational regimes.
tldr: The paper identifies the statistically optimal four-copy detector for the three-tangle and analyzes its circuit and fault-tolerant implementation costs.
motivation: The three-tangle distinguishes GHZ-type from W-type genuine tripartite entanglement, but detecting it efficiently in practice requires balancing statistical power against experimental and fault-tolerant resource overhead.
method: Using representation-theoretic structure, the authors derive the optimal one-sided four-copy three-tangle detector and construct ancilla-free CNOT circuits, including a 15-CNOT optimal detector and an 11-CNOT suboptimal detector, then estimate encoded implementation costs under Steane and [[7,1,3]]-type codes.
result: The optimal detector has higher click probability than previous four-copy constructions, reducing the required repetitions, but this statistical advantage comes with greater circuit and non-Clifford synthesis cost; early fault-tolerant implementations can reduce overhead at the price of additional encoded resources.
conclusion: There is a tradeoff between statistical efficiency and implementation cost for three-tangle detection, and this tradeoff persists in fault-tolerant settings, with explicit resource estimates quantifying the cost across computational regimes.

title: R\'enyi Multi-entropy Of Graph States And The $n -> 1$ Limit
authors: Abhijit Gadde Sriram Akella
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: R\'enyi multi-entropy extends the R\'enyi entropy to pure states of more than two parties. It is defined by a replica contraction at integer replica number [MATH], and the multi-entropy is its [MATH] limit. In holography this limit is conjectured to compute the area of a minimal soap-film web in the bulk. Understanding multi-entropy for general states, however, is harder. Unlike the bipartite case, the replica contraction is not a moment of a density matrix, and the continuation to [MATH] has to be found by other means. We study this problem for qubit graph states. We show that at every odd [MATH] the contraction equals [MATH], where [MATH] is a sum of ranks of matrices over a finite field, one row and one column per qubit. We define a class of graphs that we call collision-controlled, for which the rank sum is a polynomial in [MATH]. This class includes graphs without even cycles and all complete bipartite graphs. The natural polynomial [MATH] continuation is a finite sum over partitions of the parties. While the R\'enyi multi-entropy is non-increasing under single-qubit Pauli measurements at every odd integer [MATH], the continuation to [MATH] is not. A [MATH] measurement on one qubit of an odd ring with [MATH] qubits raises it from [MATH] to [MATH]. Thus the continuation is not an entanglement monotone.
tldr: The paper analyzes Rényi multi-entropy for qubit graph states, deriving exact replica contractions at odd integer replica numbers and studying the n→1 continuation.
motivation: Rényi multi-entropy generalizes bipartite Rényi entropy to multipartite pure states, but its analytic continuation is subtle because the replica contraction is not a density-matrix moment; graph states offer a tractable testbed.
method: The authors express the odd-integer replica contraction for graph states as a sum of ranks of matrices over finite fields, define collision-controlled graphs where this rank sum is polynomial in the replica number, and study the resulting n→1 continuation and its behavior under Pauli measurements.
result: For collision-controlled graphs, including even-cycle-free graphs and complete bipartite graphs, the rank sum admits a natural polynomial continuation given by a finite sum over party partitions; unlike the odd-integer Rényi multi-entropy, this continuation is not non-increasing under single-qubit Pauli measurements.
conclusion: The n→1 continuation of Rényi multi-entropy for graph states is not an entanglement monotone, as exemplified by a measurement on one qubit of an odd ring raising the continuation.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper studies Rényi multi-entropy for qubit graph states, a quantity that generalizes Rényi entropy to pure states of more than two parties. Multi-entropy is defined via a replica contraction at integer n, and its n→1 limit is conjectured in holography to compute the area of a minimal soap-film web. For general states, the replica contraction is not a moment of a density matrix, so the n→1 continuation is nontrivial. The authors focus on qubit graph states and show that at every odd n the contraction equals 2^{-k/2}, where k is a sum of ranks of matrices over a finite field, one row and one column per qubit. They introduce a class of 'collision-controlled' graphs for which the rank sum is a polynomial in n. This class includes graphs without even cycles and all complete bipartite graphs. The natural polynomial n→1 continuation is a finite sum over partitions of the parties. They find that while the Rényi multi-entropy is non-increasing under single-qubit Pauli measurements at every odd integer n>1, the continuation to n=1 is not: a Z measurement on one qubit of an odd ring with 2r+1≥7 qubits raises it from (r+1)log2 to (2r-1)log2. Thus the continuation is not an entanglement monotone.

The methodology combines graph theory, finite field linear algebra, and asymptotic analysis to extract the n→1 limit.

title: Stabilizer R\'enyi Moments Beyond Entanglement
authors: Joydeep Naskar Vishnu Jejjala
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stabilizer R\'enyi moments depend on a choice of operator basis and need not be determined by entanglement spectra. In this paper, we study their spatial decay in critical quantum chains described by two-dimensional conformal field theories. We derive an exact entanglement baseline for reductions of pure stabilizer states and a symmetry selection rule for the charged contribution at fixed support. An exact Ising example shows that an on-site rotation changes the full decay exponent while preserving every subsystem entanglement spectrum. For growing Ising intervals at index two, we obtain an exact Pfaffian representation and compare the charged amplitude with a candidate conformal boundary calculation. The data support this prediction, but its identification with the lattice limit still requires endpoint matching and control of the order of limits.
tldr: The paper analyzes spatial decay of stabilizer Rényi moments in critical CFT chains, showing they encode basis-dependent non-stabilizerness beyond entanglement spectra.
motivation: Stabilizer Rényi moments depend on the operator basis and are not fixed by entanglement, so their behavior in critical quantum chains needs a separate information-theoretic characterization.
method: The authors derive exact entanglement baselines for reduced pure stabilizer states and a symmetry selection rule, then study Ising intervals using exact Pfaffian representations and compare with a conformal boundary calculation.
result: An exact Ising example shows an on-site rotation can change the full decay exponent while preserving every subsystem entanglement spectrum; for growing intervals at index two, the charged amplitude matches the conformal prediction under certain limits.
conclusion: Stabilizer Rényi moments capture non-stabilizerness features not visible in entanglement alone, but a full lattice-limit identification requires endpoint matching and careful control of limits.

title: Microscopic Bipartition And Macroscopic Symmetry In A R\'enyi Entanglement Ensemble
authors: Zhe Wang, Dongxu Liu, Zheng Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal information extracted from entanglement at a critical point is commonly associated with the long-distance properties of the bulk state, while microscopic details of a lattice bipartition are expected to be washed out under coarse graining. Counterintuitively, we show directly that such microscopic information can survive in the statistical ensemble that determines the second R\'enyi entropy and obviously change the physics there. Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the square-lattice [MATH]-[MATH] model at the N\'eel--valence-bond-solid (VBS) transition, we measure magnetic and dimer order parameters in the R\'enyi-2 ensemble. For a standard axis-aligned bipartition, the VBS component perpendicular to the entanglement boundary remains finite in the thermodynamic extrapolation and is inequivalent to the parallel component, while the N\'eel order vanishes. For a [MATH] tilted bipartition, in contrast, the two VBS components remain equivalent within numerical accuracy. We interpret this contrast in terms of the R\'enyi twist defect: the two bipartitions have the same bulk theory but realize different microscopic defect symmetries. Our results demonstrate that lattice information invisible to the bulk continuum theory alone can remain active in the long-distance R\'enyi ensemble, providing a microscopic explanation for the strong bipartition dependence previously observed in entanglement studies of deconfined criticality.
tldr: The paper shows that microscopic details of a lattice bipartition can survive in the Rényi-2 entanglement ensemble and affect long-distance physics at a Néel–VBS transition.
motivation: Entanglement at critical points is usually tied to bulk universal properties, with microscopic lattice details expected to wash out under coarse graining, yet prior studies observe strong bipartition dependence in entanglement measures.
method: Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the square-lattice J-Q model at the Néel–valence-bond-solid transition, the authors measure magnetic and dimer order parameters in the Rényi-2 ensemble for axis-aligned and tilted bipartitions.
result: For axis-aligned bipartitions, the perpendicular VBS component remains finite and differs from the parallel component while Néel order vanishes; for tilted bipartitions, the two VBS components remain equivalent within numerical accuracy.
conclusion: The contrast is explained by different microscopic defect symmetries of the Rényi twist defect, demonstrating that lattice information invisible to bulk continuum theory can remain active in the long-distance Rényi ensemble and explain bipartition dependence in deconfined criticality.

They compare two bipartitions: a standard axis-aligned cut and a 45° tilted cut. For the axis-aligned bipartition, the VBS order parameter perpendicular to the entanglement boundary remains finite in the thermodynamic extrapolation and differs from the parallel component, while the Néel order vanishes. In contrast, for the tilted bipartition, the two VBS components remain equivalent within numerical accuracy. The authors interpret this contrast through the concept of a Rényi twist defect: although both bipartitions share the same bulk continuum theory, they realize different microscopic defect symmetries. This demonstrates that lattice information invisible to the bulk continuum theory can remain active in the long-distance Rényi ensemble, offering a microscopic explanation for the strong bipartition dependence previously observed in entanglement studies of deconfined criticality.

The key methodological innovation is the measurement of order parameters within the Rényi-2 ensemble, which is realized by replicating the system and introducing a twist defect along the entanglement cut. This approach allows direct access to the statistical properties of the Rényi ensemble, going beyond the usual entanglement entropy calculations. title: Low-nonlinearity Advantage Of Hollow-core Fiber For Wavelength Multiplexing Of Quantum Entanglement And Classical Dwdm Signals
authors: Hikaru Shimizu, Arisa Ohno, Mao Miyasugi, Yumeno Seki, Naoyuki Funaoka, Yukari Takada, Aruto Hosaka, Shun Fujii, Hiroyuki Tsuda, Masahiro Takeoka
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coexistence of classical and quantum light in optical fiber is a key requirement for scalable quantum networks. However, it is fundamentally limited by nonlinear crosstalk from intense classical signals. Hollow-core fiber (HCF), with its intrinsically low optical nonlinearity, offers a promising solution. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the coexistence of polarization-entangled photons with dense wavelength-division multiplexed (DWDM) classical signals with a total launch power of 11.2 dBm, and perform a direct comparison between equal-length single-mode fiber (SMF) and photonic-bandgap-based HCF deployed in a campus network. We observe that HCF suppresses background noise by approximately two orders of magnitude compared to SMF, while preserving high-fidelity entanglement distribution. Our results provide clear experimental evidence of the advantage of HCF and establish its potential as a transmission medium.
tldr: Experimental comparison showing photonic-bandgap hollow-core fiber suppresses nonlinear crosstalk from DWDM classical signals by ~two orders of magnitude relative to single-mode fiber while preserving polarization-entangled photon fidelity.
motivation: Scalable quantum networks require coexisting classical and quantum channels in the same fiber, but Kerr nonlinearity from intense classical DWDM light generates noise that fundamentally limits entanglement distribution.
method: Polarization-entangled photons were co-propagated with DWDM classical signals at 11.2 dBm total launch power through equal-length single-mode fiber and photonic-bandgap hollow-core fiber deployed in a campus network, with noise and entanglement fidelity measured for both.
result: HCF reduced background noise by roughly two orders of magnitude compared to SMF while maintaining high-fidelity entanglement distribution at the same launch power.
conclusion: The measurements give direct experimental evidence that low-nonlinearity hollow-core fiber is a superior medium for multiplexed classical-quantum transmission, supporting its use in future quantum network infrastructure.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper experimentally investigates the coexistence of polarization-entangled photons with dense wavelength-division multiplexed (DWDM) classical signals in hollow-core fiber (HCF) versus single-mode fiber (SMF). The authors deploy equal-length (likely several km) SMF and photonic-bandgap-based HCF in a campus network and compare their performance under a total classical launch power of 11.2 dBm. They measure the background noise (Raman scattering and other nonlinear crosstalk) and entanglement fidelity. The key finding is that HCF suppresses background noise by approximately two orders of magnitude relative to SMF while preserving high-fidelity entanglement distribution. This demonstrates HCF's potential as a transmission medium for scalable quantum networks where classical and quantum signals must coexist.

title: Concurrent Entanglement Purification Scheduling In Dynamic Quantum Networks
authors: Lester Ho Gongyu Ni
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum networks must deliver end-to-end entanglement whose fidelity meets application requirements, which typically requires entanglement purification along multi-hop paths. Existing scheduling approaches either purify at the link level or optimize end-to-end fidelity for a static set of requests, and do not capture concurrent requests competing for network resources over time. This paper studies concurrent entanglement purification scheduling in a time-slotted quantum network with heterogeneous links, in which requests compete for link capacity and quantum memories, and each request may be served by multiple parallel paths for increased reliability. We formulate a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler that maximizes the number of scheduled requests, with max-min path allocation as a fairness criterion, and develop reinforcement learning (RL) schedulers based on DQN, PPO, and SAC, whose rewards balance request success against Bell-pair consumption. Simulations under varying network load, topologies and target fidelity thresholds show that the RL schedulers achieve the highest success rates, improving on MILP by up to 6% and on Progressive Filling and Greedy heuristics by 16.5% and 19.5% respectively, at the cost of higher Bell pair consumption and the deferral of a small fraction of requests. MILP, in contrast, achieves the highest fairness and the lowest Bell pair consumption in most scenarios.
tldr: The paper studies concurrent entanglement purification scheduling in dynamic quantum networks using MILP and reinforcement learning schedulers.
motivation: Quantum networks need end-to-end entanglement fidelity, often requiring purification over multi-hop paths, but existing schedulers do not adequately handle concurrent requests competing for link capacity and quantum memories over time.
method: It formulates a mixed-integer linear programming scheduler maximizing scheduled requests with max-min fairness, and develops DQN, PPO, and SAC reinforcement learning schedulers that balance request success against Bell-pair consumption.
result: RL schedulers achieve the highest success rates, improving over MILP by up to 6% and over Progressive Filling and Greedy heuristics by 16.5% and 19.5%, though with higher Bell-pair consumption and some request deferral; MILP gives better fairness and lower Bell-pair use in most scenarios.
conclusion: Reinforcement learning is effective for concurrent purification scheduling in dynamic quantum networks, while MILP remains preferable when fairness and resource efficiency are prioritized.

deep_read.detailed_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of scheduling concurrent entanglement purification requests in a time-slotted quantum network with heterogeneous links, where multiple requests compete for shared link capacity and quantum memories, and each request may be served by multiple parallel paths to improve reliability. The authors formulate the problem as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler that maximizes the number of successfully scheduled requests while enforcing a max-min path allocation fairness criterion. Because MILP is computationally heavy and static, they additionally develop reinforcement learning schedulers based on DQN, PPO, and SAC, with reward functions that trade off request success against Bell-pair consumption.

The evaluation is simulation-based, sweeping network load, topology, and target fidelity thresholds. The central empirical finding is that RL schedulers achieve the highest request success rates, improving on MILP by up to 6% and on the Progressive Filling and Greedy heuristics by 16.5% and 19.5% respectively. This success comes at the cost of higher Bell-pair consumption and the deferral of a small fraction of requests. Conversely, MILP delivers the best fairness and, in most scenarios, the lowest Bell-pair consumption.

The paper thus positions RL as a throughput-oriented alternative to optimization-based scheduling for dynamic, contention-heavy quantum network scenarios, while MILP remains preferable when fairness and resource economy dominate. The work sits at the intersection of quantum network resource management and learning-based scheduling, and its main contribution is a comparative framework spanning exact optimization, heuristics, and three RL algorithms under a shared problem formulation.

A methodological concern is that the paper reports only aggregate outcome metrics (success rate, Bell-pair consumption, fairness, deferral fraction) without detailing state representation, action-space design, training convergence, or generalization across topologies. title: Assignment Maps For Arbitrary Reduced Quantum Dynamics
authors: Weixiang Ye James Fullwood
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given an open quantum system [MATH] with environment [MATH], we establish a one-to-one correspondence between completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) maps from [MATH] to [MATH] and assignment maps initializing the composite system [MATH] in a possibly correlated state prior to unitary evolution. We show that every possible joint state [MATH] can be realized by such assignment maps, which are inherently Hermiticity-preserving and trace-preserving (HPTP). While these maps sacrifice global positivity, we derive a simple necessary and sufficient condition for any local state of [MATH] to belong to their domain of validity. Furthermore, we prove that the geometry of this domain is governed by the joint state assigned to the maximally mixed input, ensuring that a non-zero volume of admissible local states can readily coexist with initial system-environment entanglement. Finally, we provide an operational protocol for witnessing such limits of validity.
tldr: The paper establishes a one-to-one correspondence between CPTP reduced dynamics and assignment maps that initialize a correlated system-environment state, and characterizes when local states remain valid under such maps.
motivation: Reduced quantum dynamics with initial system-environment correlations is subtle because standard CPTP descriptions may fail or require assumptions about the initial joint state. The authors aim to characterize arbitrary reduced dynamics via assignment maps while controlling the validity domain of local states.
method: They introduce Hermiticity-preserving trace-preserving assignment maps that initialize the composite system in a potentially correlated state before unitary evolution, and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for local states to belong to the domain of validity, including a geometric characterization via the joint state assigned to the maximally mixed input.
result: Every joint state can be realized by such assignment maps, and the validity domain has non-zero volume even in the presence of initial entanglement. An operational protocol is provided to witness the limits of validity.
conclusion: Assignment maps offer a general framework for arbitrary reduced quantum dynamics with initial correlations, clarifying the tradeoff between global positivity and the admissible set of local input states.

title: Cavity Models Of non-Abelian Gauge Theories
authors: Lucia Valor, Jacquelin Luneau, Klaus Liegener, Stefan Filipp, Peter Rabl
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In quantum optics and related fields, cavity quantum electrodynamics provides a powerful framework for modeling the low-energy properties of bound charges coupled to electromagnetic fields, using a minimal set of atomic levels and isolated photonic modes. Here, we develop a similar framework for non-Abelian gauge theories, focusing on the pure-gauge dynamics of SU(2) fields as the conceptually simplest example. Starting from the corresponding Yang-Mills Lagrangian, we derive an SU(2) cavity Hamiltonian in the Coulomb gauge, represented in terms of only three localized bosonic modes. Unlike its non-interacting electromagnetic counterpart, this model exhibits a nontrivial excitation spectrum featuring bound composite gauge particles ('glueballs') as the lowest-energy configurations. We extend this framework to one-dimensional arrays of coupled SU(2) cavities and discuss the driven excitation of a glueball condensate and the clustering of multi-glueball states as two elementary interaction-induced processes in these models. These examples offer a glimpse into the multitude of novel many-body phenomena that arise within this cavity SU(2) framework and we show how this physics at the interface between particle physics and quantum optics can be experimentally explored using state-of-the-art superconducting quantum circuits.
tldr: The paper develops a cavity-QED framework for pure SU(2) gauge theories, deriving a three-mode cavity Hamiltonian that exhibits glueball-like bound states and proposing superconducting-circuit implementations.
motivation: Cavity QED successfully models low-energy bound charges coupled to electromagnetic fields, motivating an analogous minimal-mode description of non-Abelian gauge dynamics for quantum simulation.
method: Starting from the Yang-Mills Lagrangian in Coulomb gauge, the authors derive an SU(2) cavity Hamiltonian with three localized bosonic modes and extend it to one-dimensional arrays of coupled SU(2) cavities.
result: The model shows a nontrivial excitation spectrum with composite gauge particles ('glueballs') as lowest-energy configurations, and identifies driven glueball condensation and multi-glueball clustering as elementary interaction-induced processes.
conclusion: The cavity SU(2) framework opens a route to studying many-body gauge-theory phenomena in quantum-optics platforms, with state-of-the-art superconducting circuits suggested for experimental exploration.

title: Active Isolation Of Transmon Readout With A Tunable Inductive Bridge
authors: Chunyang Ding, Chuyao Tong, Paul Varosy, Nikitha Jain, Ziyi Zhao, Eric I. Rosenthal, Konrad W. Lehnert, David I. Schuster
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable superconducting quantum computation requires fast, high-fidelity readout. Currently, this is assisted through cryogenic amplification of the readout signal. In traditional dispersive readout schemes, the amplifiers that are used to provide high signal-to-noise ratio also generate thermal noise that can decohere the qubits, demanding additional ferrite-based isolators to suppress this noise. Here, we integrate a chip-scale microwave switch, the tunable inductive bridge, into the readout chain of a fixed-frequency transmon. Flux-pulsing the switch, such that it transmits only during the readout, did not make a discernable difference to qubit coherence, residual excited-state population, or readout fidelity metrics. By injecting broadband noise that mimics amplifier thermal photons, we show that the switch suppresses the resulting qubit dephasing by more than [MATH]~dB, consistent with its independently measured on-off ratio, establishing it as a potential chip-based integrated replacement for readout-chain isolators.
tldr: The paper integrates a chip-scale tunable inductive bridge into a transmon readout chain as an active microwave isolator to suppress amplifier-induced thermal noise.
motivation: Cryogenic amplifiers used for high-fidelity superconducting qubit readout generate thermal noise that can dephase qubits, requiring bulky ferrite isolators that hinder scalability.
method: A tunable inductive bridge microwave switch is flux-pulsed to transmit only during readout and is inserted into the readout chain of a fixed-frequency transmon; broadband noise injection mimics amplifier thermal photons.
result: Flux-pulsing the switch caused no discernible change in qubit coherence, residual excited-state population, or readout fidelity, while suppressing noise-induced dephasing by more than [MATH]~dB, consistent with its independently measured on-off ratio.
conclusion: The tunable inductive bridge is a promising chip-integrated replacement for readout-chain isolators in scalable superconducting quantum processors.

To quantify the switch's isolation, they inject broadband noise mimicking amplifier thermal photons and measure a suppression of qubit dephasing by more than 30 dB, consistent with the switch's independently measured on-off ratio. title: Choi-Jamio{\l}kowski Isomorphism(s) And Channel/state Duality, Naturally!
authors: Paul E. Lammert
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Provided a maximally entangled state vector in [MATH], the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism of quantum information theory (or channel/state duality) produces a mapping of [MATH] (completely positive maps of density operators on [MATH] tothose on [MATH]) onto the density operators on [MATH], which extends to a unitary map. Here, [MATH] and [MATH] are {finite-dimensional} Hilbert spaces.The nature of this construction, the form of the associated formulas, and the possibility of versions which do not require an entangled vector seed, are illuminated from the perspective of {naturality}, in the sense of Eilenberg and MacLane.There is a unique such correspondence (``Choi map'') natural in both [MATH] and [MATH] which produces density operators on either [MATH] (Hilbert-Schmidt inner product) or [MATH] instead of [MATH]. In particular, no entangled state input is required. There are no such binatural maps carried on [MATH], but those natural in only [MATH] are canonically associated with unitary maps [MATH] and derive from the binatural maps. The construction recovers the standard Choi-Jamiolkowski formulae and shows how they express naturality.

method: The author analyzes completely positive maps and density operators through natural transformations between functors of finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, comparing binatural maps and maps natural in only one argument.
result: A unique Choi map natural in both Hilbert spaces is identified, producing density operators on either tensor factor under suitable inner products, and no entangled-state input is required. The standard Choi-Jamiolkowski formulas are recovered and interpreted as expressions of naturality.
conclusion: The construction provides a conceptual foundation for channel/state duality and clarifies which categorical naturality conditions single out the Choi correspondence. It is a mathematically deep structural result rather than a direct application to entanglement, cryptography, or thermodynamics.

title: Field Demonstration Of A Self-contained 10 Km Mobile-to-ground Quantum Network Node Via Common-aperture Co-propagation
authors: Dongkyu Kim, Dong-Gil Im, Kyungdeuk Park, Jisu Kim, Jonguk Choi, Yonggi Jo, Yong Sup Ihn
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we demonstrate a dual-function, common-aperture free-space optical system that simultaneously supports decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) at 803 nm and bidirectional classical laser communication at 640/660 nm over a 10.31 km terrestrial link from a mobile platform to a stationary ground station. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first field demonstration of a fully integrated common-aperture architecture where a co-propagating classical optical link simultaneously performs full QKD post-processing and ecrypted payload transmission over a 10 km atmospheric channel. The classical link utilizes Manchester-coded on-off keying (MC-OOK) at 10 MHz, achieving a packet error rate of [MATH] 0.4 [MATH] (estimated bit error rate (BER) of 3.13 [MATH] 10[MATH]) with hardware-based self-synchronization and error-packet retransmission. Over the 10.31 km link, the QKD system achieved an average quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 2.512 [MATH] and an average secret key rate of 644 bps using rate-adaptive low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Finally, using the distilled keys, real-time AES-256 encrypted image transmission was executed over the co-aligned classical optical channel, proving the feasibility of a completely self-contained, jam resistant mobile quantum optical network.

conclusion: The demonstration shows feasibility of a fully integrated, jam-resistant mobile quantum optical network node combining QKD post-processing and encrypted classical payload transmission in a single common-aperture architecture.

title: Single-photon Time Qubit: Quantum-vacuum Control And Complementarity Of The Arrow Of Time
authors: Tai Hyun Yoon
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Treating the arrow of time as a controllable quantum variable rather than a fixed external parameter is a central challenge in quantum physics. Recently, Bloch~ proposed the theoretical concept of a , a two-level control space [MATH] that selects between opposite Hamiltonian evolutions [MATH], but this paradigm has remained experimentally unrealized. Here we formulate the quantum-optical theory of a single-photon time qubit---uncovering quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time---and experimentally probe and validate its predictions using phase-resolved single-photon interferometry from two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources~. First, we show theoretically and verify experimentally that a controlled [MATH] pump--seed phase inversion during pair creation from the quantum vacuum flips the stimulated displacement generator [MATH] on top of the spontaneous two-mode squeezing background [MATH], reversing the stimulated evolution time [[MATH]] and enabling universal single-qubit [MATH] control and postselection-free first-order tomography on the temporal Bloch sphere. Second, we prove that spontaneous idler vacuum fluctuations record complete which-branch (temporal-direction) information whereas the shared coherent seed erases it without cascading or aligning the idler beams, establishing an exact wave--particle complementarity law [MATH] for the purity of the arrow of time and enabling direct first-order measurement of the Loschmidt time-reversal echo.
tldr: The paper theoretically formulates and experimentally demonstrates a single-photon time qubit in which the arrow of time is controlled via quantum-vacuum and pump-seed phase operations, revealing a complementarity law between temporal-direction information and interference.
motivation: Bloch's proposal to treat the arrow of time as a controllable two-level quantum variable had not been experimentally realized, motivating a quantum-optical implementation and test of time-qubit control and temporal complementarity.
method: The authors develop a quantum-optical theory of a single-photon time qubit and probe it using phase-resolved single-photon interferometry with two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources, including controlled pump-seed phase inversion during pair creation.
result: They experimentally verify reversal of the stimulated evolution time and universal single-qubit control on the temporal Bloch sphere, and they establish an exact wave-particle complementarity law for the purity of the arrow of time using idler vacuum fluctuations versus coherent seed erasure of which-branch information.
conclusion: The work realizes a controllable single-photon time qubit and provides a first-order measurement of the Loschmidt time-reversal echo, advancing fundamental quantum control and complementarity studies with potential relevance to quantum information processing.

The authors develop a quantum-optical theory showing that a controlled π pump–seed phase inversion during pair creation flips the stimulated displacement generator V → −V on top of the spontaneous two-mode squeezing background H0, effectively reversing the stimulated evolution time: U_stim,−(t) = U_stim,+(−t). This enables universal single-qubit SU(2) control and postselection-free first-order tomography on the temporal Bloch sphere. They further prove an exact wave–particle complementarity law |r| = V = |α|²/(1+|α|²) for the purity of the arrow of time, where spontaneous idler vacuum fluctuations record complete which-branch information while the shared coherent seed erases it without cascading or aligning the idler beams. Experimentally, they validate these predictions using two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources, demonstrating direct first-order measurement of the Loschmidt time-reversal echo. The work establishes a new paradigm for treating the arrow of time as a controllable quantum variable, with implications for quantum information, metrology, and fundamental tests of time-reversal symmetry.

title: Engineering \(xy\) And \(zz\) Interactions Between Two Remote Superconducting Qubits Via A Multimode Waveguide
authors: Yu-Xi Liu Da-Wei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Waveguides provide a flexible platform for long-range interactions between superconducting qubits. Here, we study how to engineer the effective \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions between two qubits via qubit frequency assignments and multimode interference determined by the mode configuration and standing-wave parities of a finite multimode waveguide. For a single-mode waveguide, we find that \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions cannot be simultaneously suppressed to zero and the residual qubit-qubit coupling always exists. For example, the \(XY\) interaction may be suppressed to a negligible level when two qubits and the waveguide mode satisfy the two-photon resonant condition, but the \(ZZ\) interaction cannot be switched off. For multimode configurations within the central dispersive window, the engineered interaction types are very different for odd and even numbers of modes. Even-mode configurations can readily produce strong \(XY\) interactions, whereas odd-mode configurations can strongly suppress the \(XY\) interaction while retaining a finite \(ZZ\) interaction. Full-Hamiltonian simulations of minimal two- and three-mode configurations confirm \(XY\)-dominated SWAP dynamics and \(ZZ\)-dominated CZ-type dynamics, respectively. These results establish a frequency assignment criterion of qubits and waveguide modes for selectively engineering long-range qubit-qubit interaction types induced by the waveguide with finite multimode.
tldr: The paper derives frequency-assignment and mode-configuration criteria for selectively engineering XY (SWAP-type) versus ZZ (CZ-type) effective couplings between two superconducting qubits mediated by a finite multimode waveguide.
motivation: Waveguide-mediated long-range coupling is a promising route to scalable superconducting architectures, but residual unwanted couplings (notably always-on ZZ) limit gate fidelities; a systematic understanding of how mode structure controls interaction type is needed.
method: Effective Hamiltonian analysis of two qubits coupled through a standing-wave multimode waveguide, using dispersive central-window regime arguments plus full-Hamiltonian numerical simulations of minimal two- and three-mode configurations.
result: Single-mode waveguides cannot simultaneously null XY and ZZ; even-mode multimode configurations yield strong XY with suppressed ZZ, whereas odd-mode configurations suppress XY while retaining finite ZZ, confirmed by SWAP-dominated and CZ-dominated dynamics in simulations.
conclusion: A concrete criterion linking qubit frequencies and waveguide mode parity to the engineered interaction type is established, enabling selective long-range XY or ZZ couplings in multimode waveguide-mediated superconducting qubit architectures.

title: Hybrid Lattice Surgery Between Smooth Boundaries
authors: Grace Ding, Yanzhu Chen, Sheng-Jie Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop smooth hybrid lattice surgery for group surface codes, enabling joint logical measurements through merge and split operations along smooth boundaries. The code patches may correspond to identical or different finite groups, including non-Abelian groups. Our central result is that smooth merge and split realize a logical [MATH]-coset measurement, where [MATH] is the subgroup defining the interface. This generalizes the joint logical parity measurement of ordinary surface codes. Using a tensor-network representation, we derive explicit measurement circuits and develop procedures for correcting nonidentity measurement outcomes. title: Parallel Omnidirectional Atom Rearrangement With Dynamic Holograms
authors: Samuel A. Engel, Dewei Gong, Ziguang Lin, Lysander Christakis, Kang-Kuen Ni, Norman Y. Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to assemble and reconfigure individual atoms is central to performing quantum science using optical tweezer arrays. Here, we demonstrate parallel omnidirectional atom transport and rearrangement using dynamic holograms generated by a single kilohertz-rate spatial light modulator. By carefully characterizing survival and heating, we show that atoms remain confined even when successive holograms are commanded before the liquid crystal has settled, enabling significantly faster transport. To generate holograms in real time, we develop and implement a warm-start, weighted Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm that achieves performance comparable to neural-network methods without requiring any training. Combining these techniques, we assemble ytterbium atoms into a 2078-site kagome lattice with 99.0% mean filling. In addition, we demonstrate parallel transport between array layers, combining axial and transverse motion to reconfigure atoms in three dimensions. Our approach is readily adaptable to existing tweezer platforms and provides a method for large-scale SLM-based atom assembly as well as programmable three-dimensional control.

motivation: Large-scale, reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays are a key platform for quantum simulation and computing, but fast, flexible atom transport is limited by the slow settling time of liquid-crystal SLMs and by hologram-generation latency.
method: They drive a single kHz-rate SLM with a warm-start, weighted Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm that produces holograms in real time (matching neural-network approaches without training), and they characterize atom survival and heating even when successive holograms are commanded before the liquid crystal settles; they also combine axial and transverse motion for three-dimensional layer-to-layer transport.
result: Atoms remain confined under the faster, non-settled transport protocol, enabling significantly faster rearrangement, and the approach assembles a 2078-site kagome lattice with 99.0% mean filling as well as parallel 3D reconfiguration between array layers.
conclusion: The technique is readily adaptable to existing tweezer platforms and provides a scalable, training-free route to large-scale SLM-based atom assembly and programmable three-dimensional control of neutral-atom arrays.

title: Comparative Optical Spectroscopy Of Er$^{3+}$, Tm$^{3+}$, And Eu$^{3+}$ Molecular Complexes At Cryogenic Temperature
authors: Farhad Rasekh, Sahil, Arsalan Mansourzadeh, Diogo Alves G\'alico, David Hunger, Muralee Murugesu, Daniel Oblak
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rare-earth molecular complexes are attracting increasing interest for quantum information applications because of their structural flexibility and chemical tunability. Here, we compare the cryogenic optical properties of Er[MATH], Tm[MATH], and Eu[MATH] complexes in the same ligand environment. Optical spectroscopy shows differing behavior across the three systems: spectral hole burning is observed in the Eu[MATH] complex, whereas no measurable hole is detected in the Er[MATH] and Tm[MATH] complexes. We measure laser-induced local heating and rethermalization in the Er[MATH] and Tm[MATH] powder-like samples, observing strong local heating and slow thermal relaxation in the cold-plate cryostat. The recovery occurs over several seconds and, for some Er[MATH] excitation conditions, extends over tens of seconds. The comparison across the three ions nevertheless suggests that heating alone is unlikely to account for the full contrast. Rather, the different behaviors of Eu[MATH], Tm[MATH], and Er[MATH] point to ion-dependent relaxation and decoherence processes associated with their electronic level structure and coupling to the molecular environment. Temperature-dependent linewidth and line-shift measurements are further consistent with phonon-mediated broadening through coupling to crystal-field levels.
tldr: Cryogenic optical spectroscopy compares Er, Tm, and Eu molecular complexes, finding spectral hole burning only in Eu and strong ion-dependent heating and decoherence effects relevant to rare-earth quantum memories.
motivation: Rare-earth molecular complexes are chemically tunable platforms of interest for quantum information, but their cryogenic optical coherence and heating behavior need comparative characterization.
method: The authors perform cryogenic optical spectroscopy on Er, Tm, and Eu complexes in the same ligand environment, including spectral hole burning, laser-induced local heating and rethermalization measurements, and temperature-dependent linewidth and line-shift measurements.
result: Spectral hole burning is observed in the Eu complex but not in Er or Tm; Er and Tm samples show strong local laser heating and slow thermal recovery over seconds to tens of seconds, while linewidth and line-shift data indicate phonon-mediated broadening.
conclusion: Heating alone does not explain the full contrast between ions; the differing behaviors point to ion-dependent relaxation and decoherence tied to electronic structure and molecular-environment coupling, with implications for rare-earth molecular quantum memory platforms.

deep_read.detailed_summary:
This paper reports a comparative cryogenic optical study of three trivalent rare-earth molecular complexes—Er3+, Tm3+, and Eu3+—prepared in the same ligand environment, with the goal of assessing their suitability as quantum-information-relevant optical materials. The central experimental contrast is that spectral hole burning (SHB), a hallmark of long optical coherence and a prerequisite for many quantum memory and single-photon protocols, is observed in the Eu3+ complex but is absent (no measurable hole) in the Er3+ and Tm3+ complexes. The authors then investigate whether laser-induced heating could explain this contrast, since the Er3+ and Tm3+ samples are powder-like and exhibit strong local heating with slow rethermalization in the cold-plate cryostat. Recovery times are on the order of several seconds, and for some Er3+ excitation conditions extend to tens of seconds.

The authors argue that heating alone is unlikely to account for the full contrast between the ions, because the magnitude and timescale of the thermal effects do not map cleanly onto the presence or absence of hole burning. Instead, they attribute the ion-dependent behavior to differences in electronic level structure and coupling to the molecular environment, which produce different relaxation and decoherence pathways. Supporting temperature-dependent linewidth and line-shift measurements are interpreted as consistent with phonon-mediated broadening via coupling to crystal-field levels.

The work is essentially a comparative, phenomenology-oriented study rather than a quantitative coherence metrology paper: it does not report measured optical coherence times (T2), homogeneous linewidths extracted from photon echoes, or hole linewidths in frequency units. Its value lies in the systematic side-by-side comparison under a common ligand framework and in flagging laser heating as a confound that must be controlled in cryogenic spectroscopy of rare-earth molecular powders.

Because Eu3+ is a non-Kramers ion with a singlet ground state and weak spin-orbit/ligand coupling relative to Kramers ions like Er3+ and Tm3+, this contrast is physically reasonable and consistent with the broader literature on rare-earth quantum memories, where Eu3+ systems are favored for long optical coherence. The temperature-dependent linewidth and line-shift trends are consistent with phonon-mediated broadening via crystal-field levels, which supports the ion-dependent decoherence picture, but the paper stops short of extracting activation energies or Debye/Raman coefficients. title: Resolving Nonlocal State Reduction Via Induced Coherence In Frequency-Comb Biphoton Sources
authors: Tai Hyun Yoon
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How macroscopic definite outcomes and nonlocal correlations emerge from entangled superpositions across spacelike-separated regions without superluminal action or {\it ad hoc} wavefunction collapse remains a defining open question in the foundations of quantum mechanics. Here, we resolve this century-long paradox within relativistic quantum electrodynamics by developing an open-system and measurement-defined framework realized in dual, spacelike-separated nonlinear crystals driven synchronously by a multi-mode optical frequency comb and seeded by an ultra-narrow coherent laser. Expanding the transverse electromagnetic vector potential into discrete single-photon frequency-comb supermodes, we show that tracing out the unmeasured continuous-wave idler field yields an exact spatial dephasing Lindblad master equation whose decoherence rate is governed by the non-orthogonal state overlap of single-photon-added coherent states. Connecting this open-system map to free-vector-space quotient measurement theory, we demonstrate that single-particle interference arises from the geometric projection of the composite state onto detector-defined conditional cosets rather than remote collapse, establishing strict operational equivalence across pump, seed, and signal phase scans. The resulting wave-particle-entanglement triality equality [MATH] is saturated across the complete parameter space, while the atomic-clock-referenced comb structure anchors continuous-variable time-frequency displacement stabilizers directly at the hardware layer. Our work unifies induced coherence, Bohr's complementarity, and quotient measurement theory, providing a microscopic pathway toward fault-tolerant bosonic quantum information processing.

method: The author expands the transverse electromagnetic vector potential into discrete frequency-comb supermodes, traces out the unmeasured idler field to derive a spatial dephasing Lindblad master equation, and connects this map to quotient measurement theory in dual spacelike-separated nonlinear crystals.
result: The framework shows that single-particle interference arises from geometric projection onto detector-defined conditional cosets, with operational equivalence across pump, seed, and signal phase scans and a saturated wave-particle-entanglement triality equality.
conclusion: The work unifies induced coherence, Bohr complementarity, and quotient measurement theory, suggesting a microscopic route toward fault-tolerant bosonic quantum information processing.

title: The Next Phase Of Quantum Energy Science: From Mechanisms To Applications
authors: Florian Metzler, Matt K. Lilley, Matthew C. Decapua, Peter L. Hagelstein, Jonah F. Messinger, Nicola Galvanetto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A growing research community spanning quantum batteries, molecular and excitonic energy transport, polaritonics, quantum materials and nuclear control has begun to describe its work in terms of quantum energy or quantum energy science. What connects these otherwise disparate efforts is the deliberate use of quantum states, couplings, collective effects and engineered environments to control energetic states and pathways. A key difference from quantum information science is that the complete quantum state does not always need to be preserved; engineered dissipation or dephasing can even improve the desired outcome. We organize this emerging domain through a framework that connects mechanisms, functions, capabilities, and applications. We identify five elementary functions (Excite, Hold, Release, Transfer, and Transform) and examine the mechanisms that implement them. The same functions recur from the molecular to the nuclear scale, although their relative implementation difficulty can differ sharply. Moving toward technology, we highlight three engineering capabilities (Storage, Routing, and Conversion) through the performance metrics that matter for their applications. Stretch scenarios illustrate what performance targets could make these capabilities technologically consequential.
tldr: This perspective proposes a unifying framework for 'quantum energy science' by connecting mechanisms, functions, engineering capabilities, and applications across quantum batteries, energy transport, polaritonics, quantum materials, and nuclear control.

title: Quantum Fluctuations And Wigner Dynamics Of A Carbon Nanotube Oscillator Driven By An Atomic Force Microscope
authors: Cristian Staii Conrad Silio
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Suspended carbon nanotubes provide a useful platform for studying controlled nanomechanical motion in regimes where environmental fluctuations, memory effects, and quantum coherence can all influence the dynamics. We model the fundamental flexural mode of a carbon nanotube driven by an atomic force microscope as a harmonic quantum Brownian oscillator subject to a prescribed classical force and coupled linearly to a thermal environment. Starting from the generalized Langevin equation, we formulate the reduced dynamics directly in phase space, where the Wigner function evolves through a Gaussian propagator determined by dissipative linear transport, a deterministic force-induced displacement, and bath-induced fluctuations. For a Drude memory kernel, the retarded response is expressed through the three roots of a characteristic cubic equation. In the classical-noise limit, the three independent entries of the finite-time covariance matrix reduce to explicit finite sums over these response poles, eliminating numerical double-time covariance integration. We extend the construction to the full quantum fluctuation spectrum, obtaining a thermal frequency series representation that retains zero-point and low-temperature fluctuations. For an initial two-packet superposition, we examine interference attenuation and the integrated negative part of the Wigner function, which provides a phase space measure of nonclassicality. These results provide an explicit analytical framework for finite-memory quantum Brownian motion of bound oscillators and a tractable phase space description of driven carbon nanotube dynamics relevant to future quantum state preparation and quantum tomography experiments.
tldr: The paper develops an analytical phase-space framework for a driven carbon-nanotube nanomechanical oscillator modeled as a quantum Brownian particle with finite memory.
motivation: Suspended carbon nanotubes offer a platform for studying controlled nanomechanical motion where environmental fluctuations, memory effects, and quantum coherence influence dynamics.
method: The authors model the fundamental flexural mode as a harmonic quantum Brownian oscillator coupled linearly to a thermal bath and derive Wigner-function dynamics via a Gaussian propagator for a Drude memory kernel.
result: They obtain explicit finite-sum expressions for the covariance matrix in the classical-noise limit and a thermal frequency-series representation for the full quantum fluctuation spectrum, then analyze interference attenuation and Wigner negativity for an initial two-packet superposition.
conclusion: The work provides a tractable analytical description of finite-memory quantum Brownian motion and phase-space nonclassicality for driven carbon-nanotube oscillators, with potential relevance to future quantum state preparation and tomography.

title: Fate Of Discrete Time Crystals In Finite-Size Cavity Qed Systems
authors: David R. Reichman Haimi Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It has been shown that Discrete Time Crystal (DTC) behavior may arise in the periodically driven, open Dicke model in the thermodynamic limit ([MATH]). In this work, we demonstrate that finite [MATH] non-mean-field fluctuations in this model can lead to decay rates and amplitudes of transient DTCs that display a non-trivial non-monotonic behavior with an increasing number of atoms. We show that the second-order cumulant expansion fails to capture the finite-size dynamics, while a stochastic version of the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA) is remarkably accurate, particularly in the large atom ensemble limit. Using the TWA and the Monte Carlo Wave Function (MCWF) approach, we identify three distinct dynamical regimes of transient DTC behavior in the finite-size Dicke model. We outline the mechanism behind the non-monotonic finite size dynamical decay of DTC order and discuss the implications for experiments performed on finite-sized atomic assemblies.
tldr: The paper studies how finite-size fluctuations modify transient discrete time crystal behavior in a periodically driven open Dicke model relevant to cavity QED experiments.
motivation: Discrete time crystals have been predicted in the thermodynamic limit of driven open Dicke models, but finite-size effects in realistic atomic ensembles may significantly alter their decay and observability.
method: The authors analyze finite-size dynamics using a stochastic Truncated Wigner Approximation and Monte Carlo Wave Function approach, comparing these with a second-order cumulant expansion that fails to capture the finite-size behavior.
result: They find non-monotonic dependence of DTC decay rates and amplitudes on atom number and identify three distinct dynamical regimes of transient DTC behavior in the finite-size Dicke model.
conclusion: Finite-size non-mean-field fluctuations qualitatively affect DTC lifetimes and should be accounted for in experiments on finite atomic assemblies; TWA is accurate in the large-ensemble limit.

title: Orchestrating Key Scarcity: Global Capacity Allocation In Hybrid Qkd-pqc Networks
authors: Pablo P. Rejo, Manuel Fern\'andez-Veiga, Ana Fern\'andez-Vilas, Diego Cajaraville-Aboy, Javier Vecino-Pe\~nas, Rebeca P. D\'iaz-Redondo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article presents a Distributed Key Management System (DKMS) that provisions quantum-safe symmetric encryption keys to applications across a network. To overcome the distance and rate limitations inherent to Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), the architecture adopts a hybrid design: it utilizes multi-hop trusted relays for physical key transport, while applying an end-to-end Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) layer to ensure the relayed key material remains strictly protected from intermediate nodes. Because QKD transforms key generation into a scarce physical resource, managing unpredictable application demands poses a critical capacity allocation problem. The core contribution of this work is an SDN-driven control plane that globally orchestrates the network. Rather than relying on vulnerable hop-by-hop capacity reservations, a central controller simultaneously computes optimal filling rates and multipath routing for all per-peer key buffers. This global orchestration ensures that no application is starved and that all key buffers synchronize their filling processes. Evaluated on a Kubernetes-based digital twin across five distinct network topologies, the controller successfully filled all key buffers to capacity in under six minutes. Furthermore, under deliberately excessive demand, the network demonstrated graceful degradation, safely rejecting excess requests through controlled rate-limiting rather than experiencing catastrophic failure.
tldr: A distributed key management system with an SDN-based global controller that optimally allocates scarce QKD-generated key material in hybrid QKD-PQC networks.
motivation: QKD is distance- and rate-limited, turning key generation into a scarce physical resource, so unpredictable application demand creates a hard capacity-allocation problem that hop-by-hop reservations handle poorly.
method: The authors build a DKMS combining multi-hop trusted relays for key transport with an end-to-end PQC protection layer, and a centralized SDN control plane that jointly computes buffer filling rates and multipath routing for all per-peer key buffers, validated on a Kubernetes digital twin over five topologies.
result: The controller filled all key buffers to capacity in under six minutes and, under excessive demand, degraded gracefully via rate-limiting rather than failing catastrophically.
conclusion: Global orchestration of key buffers outperforms local reservation schemes, but the contribution is network-systems engineering rather than a quantum information or protocol-theoretic advance.

title: Systematic Truncated Wigner Approximation For Open Spin Systems Reveals Long-Range Order Far From Equilibrium
authors: Igor Timofeev, Dawid A. Hryniuk, Marzena H. Szyma\'nska
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-range interactions can protect dissipative order against fluctuations, but determining when they do so in two dimensions remains out of reach for existing many-body methods. We develop a continuous SU(2)-covariant truncated-Wigner framework that maps the problem onto stochastic dynamics with one Bloch sphere per site. Derived systematically from the exact Stratonovich-Weyl evolution of the Lindblad equation, it generates both drift and reservoir noise for arbitrary spin [MATH]. Benchmarks against exact and tensor-network calculations validate its description of non-equilibrium dynamics and steady states. Applied to 400-site two-dimensional dissipative anisotropic XY lattices, our method reveals physics missed by mean-field and perturbative approaches: vortex-antivortex proliferation destroys the predicted staggered-XY phase for nearest-neighbour coupling, whereas algebraically decaying interactions stabilize an extended [MATH]-ordered phase. We obtain the first beyond-mean-field steady-state phase diagram of the long-range interacting model, revealing reentrant loss of order at strong coupling and closure of the ordered region beyond [MATH]. Our new method provides a scalable route to strongly correlated driven-dissipative systems with long-range interactions, higher-dimensional geometries, spin-boson couplings, and spins beyond one half, relevant to modern experiments with magnetic atoms and polar molecules in optical lattices and tweezer arrays.
tldr: A truncated-Wigner framework for open spin systems reveals beyond-mean-field steady-state phases in two-dimensional long-range dissipative XY lattices.
motivation: Long-range interactions can protect dissipative order against fluctuations, but existing many-body methods cannot resolve when this occurs in two dimensions.
method: The authors derive a continuous SU(2)-covariant stochastic Wigner dynamics systematically from the Stratonovich-Weyl representation of the Lindblad equation and benchmark it against exact and tensor-network calculations.
result: For 400-site 2D dissipative anisotropic XY lattices, vortex-antivortex proliferation destroys the staggered-XY phase for nearest-neighbor coupling, while algebraically decaying interactions stabilize an extended ordered phase, with reentrant loss of order at strong coupling.
conclusion: The method provides a scalable route to strongly correlated driven-dissipative spin systems with long-range interactions, relevant to optical-lattice and tweezer-array experiments.

title: Polynomial-Time Classical Simulation Of BosonSampling Under Any Constant-Fraction Photon Loss
authors: Hyunseok Jeong Byeongseon Go
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how photon loss changes the classical complexity of BosonSampling is central to assessing the robustness of near-term photonic quantum advantage. In this work, we present a polynomial-time classical simulation algorithm for lossy BosonSampling that applies whenever a constant fraction of the input photons survives. We consider the standard fixed-loss model, where [MATH] input photons propagate through an [MATH]-mode interferometer and exactly [MATH] photons are lost uniformly at random, leaving [MATH] surviving photons at the output. For any constant surviving fraction [MATH], the algorithm samples from a distribution within total variation distance [MATH] of the fixed-loss BosonSampling distribution with probability at least [MATH] over Haar-random interferometers, in time [MATH]. We further extend the fixed-loss analysis to the uniform-transmission-loss model and obtain analogous polynomial-time simulability for any fixed transmission rate [MATH]. These results substantially extend the known provably simulable regime of [MATH] surviving photons or [MATH] transmission rate, and demonstrate that even the experimentally relevant linear-survival regime can admit efficient classical simulation under the conditions considered here.
tldr: This paper gives a polynomial-time classical simulation algorithm for BosonSampling when any constant fraction of input photons survives or transmission rate is constant.
motivation: Photon loss is a major obstacle to photonic quantum advantage, so understanding whether lossy BosonSampling remains classically hard is important for assessing near-term quantum advantage claims.
method: The authors analyze fixed-loss BosonSampling, where a constant fraction of photons is lost uniformly at random, and extend the analysis to a uniform-transmission-loss model, constructing a classical sampling algorithm for these regimes.
result: For any constant surviving fraction or fixed transmission rate, the algorithm samples within total variation distance epsilon of the lossy BosonSampling distribution with high probability over Haar-random interferometers in polynomial time.
conclusion: The provably simulable regime of BosonSampling is substantially extended, showing that even the experimentally relevant linear-survival regime can admit efficient classical simulation under the considered conditions.

title: Allight: A Perfect Photon Collector
authors: Dan Porat, Ran Finkelstein, Tal Carmon
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collecting photons from quantum emitters remains a key limitation in light-matter interaction because conventional lenses collect light only from one direction. Here, we introduce a perfect light collector by inverse-designing a surrounding dielectric structure that encloses the emitter to increase photon-collection efficiency toward unity. Decomposing the device into several refractive interfaces enables emission collection from the full 4[MATH] solid angle with adiabatic reshaping into a collimated beam. We experimentally demonstrate, in two dimensions, the ray bending that collimates omnidirectional emission. Our collector transforms current paradigms for highly efficient photon collection from narrowband, cavity-based techniques into experimentally robust, broadband, non-resonant dielectric devices.
tldr: An inverse-designed dielectric enclosure collects omnidirectional emission from quantum emitters and reshapes it into a collimated beam with near-unity collection efficiency.
motivation: Conventional lenses collect light from only one direction, limiting photon-collection efficiency in light-matter interaction and quantum-emitter interfaces.
method: The device is decomposed into multiple refractive interfaces surrounding the emitter to capture the full 4π solid angle and adiabatically reshape the emission into a collimated beam; a two-dimensional experimental demonstration of ray bending and collimation is presented.
result: The authors experimentally demonstrate omnidirectional emission collimation in two dimensions using a broadband, non-resonant dielectric structure, moving photon collection toward unity efficiency.
conclusion: This work offers a robust, broadband alternative to narrowband cavity-based photon-collection techniques, with potential relevance to quantum-emitter light-matter interfaces.

title: The Optical Force On A Dielectric Slab
authors: Andrew Laeuger, Kevin Kuns, Yanbei Chen, Nancy Aggarwal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radiation-pressure forces on transmissive optics, including dynamical backaction, are usually computed from the momentum flux of the external fields. For a dielectric of finite thickness, this omits the time dependence of the electromagnetic momentum stored inside. We compute the force on a lossless dielectric slab of arbitrary thickness [MATH] submerged in a dielectric fluid, proceeding from both Lorentz force on its bound charges and from the external momentum fluxes for arbitrary carrier and sideband fields. We treat the surrounding medium through a prescribed linear dielectric response and do not model the accompanying mechanical response of the fluid, including pressure and electrostriction. These two methods both recover the expected force in the limit of a thin reflector, but differ in the more general case by the rate of change of the field momentum stored in the slab. This storage term vanishes for static fields and at low frequencies reduces to [MATH], where [MATH] is the net power through the slab. In a cavity, where [MATH] depends on the slab position, the storage term produces a velocity-dependent force. The Abraham and Minkowski momentum formulations applied to the storage term are reconciled to give an unambiguous force on the dielectric in the case of an exterior vacuum environment, where there is no fluid response to model.
tldr: The paper derives the radiation-pressure force on a lossless dielectric slab of arbitrary thickness by comparing the Lorentz-force approach with the external momentum-flux approach, showing they differ by the rate of change of electromagnetic momentum stored inside the slab.
motivation: Standard treatments of radiation pressure and dynamical backaction on transmissive optics compute forces from external field momentum fluxes, which neglects the time dependence of momentum stored in a finite-thickness dielectric — a potentially important omission for precision optomechanics such as interferometric gravitational-wave detectors.
method: Two independent calculations are performed for a slab of arbitrary thickness immersed in a dielectric fluid: a direct Lorentz force on bound charges, and an external momentum-flux ( Maxwell stress) calculation, for arbitrary carrier and sideband fields, with the surrounding medium treated via a prescribed linear dielectric response.
result: Both methods agree in the thin-reflector limit but differ in general by the storage term, the rate of change of field momentum inside the slab; this term vanishes for static fields and at low frequencies reduces to a power-proportional contribution, producing a velocity-dependent force in a cavity where the stored momentum depends on slab position.
conclusion: Including the internal momentum storage term is necessary for a consistent force on thick dielectric slabs, and the Abraham and Minkowski formulations are reconciled to give an unambiguous force when the exterior environment is vacuum and no fluid response must be modeled.

title: Shot Allocation Strategies In Debugging Quantum Circuits
authors: Era Thaqi, Coco Gong, Margaret Martonosi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Debugging quantum programs remains challenging due to the nature of quantum measurement. As quantum algorithms and systems scale, it is increasingly crucial to develop rigorous debugging and verification approaches. Statistical assertion-based debugging validates quantum program behavior through repeated circuit execution and statistical hypothesis testing, but existing frameworks treat shot count as a fixed input parameter, leaving the problem of optimal shot allocation across multiple mid-circuit assertions unexplored. To improve debugging efficiency by making better use of given shot counts, this paper proposes and evaluates four shot allocation strategies within the QDB quantum debugger implemented within the CUDA-Q framework. These allocation approaches: equal split, static weight allocation, adaptive entropy routing, and sequential retirement, use statistical approaches to test whether qubits have expected state characteristics at different points in execution. We evaluate these allocation strategies on different circuits, under both noise-free and depolarizing noise conditions. We show how adaptive strategies use shots efficiently by concentrating them on assertions with high uncertainty. This substantially reduces total shot usage while maintaining comparable debugging confidence.
tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates four shot allocation strategies for statistical assertion-based debugging of quantum circuits within the QDB debugger in CUDA-Q.
motivation: Debugging quantum programs is difficult because measurement is destructive and statistical assertion-based methods require repeated circuit executions, but existing frameworks treat shot count as fixed and do not optimize allocation across multiple mid-circuit assertions.
method: The authors implement equal split, static weight allocation, adaptive entropy routing, and sequential retirement strategies in the QDB quantum debugger and evaluate them on several circuits under noise-free and depolarizing noise conditions.
result: Adaptive strategies concentrate shots on assertions with high uncertainty, substantially reducing total shot usage while maintaining comparable debugging confidence.
conclusion: Optimized shot allocation can improve the efficiency of statistical quantum program debugging, though the contribution is primarily practical debugger engineering rather than a core information-theoretic advance.

title: Collision-aware Bayesian Mitigation Of Photon Loss In Linear Optical Quantum Circuits
authors: Seungwoo Kim, Seunghyun Ahn, Donguk Nam, Hyunho Cha, Jungwoo Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photon loss is the dominant noise source in linear optical quantum circuits. Each lost photon turns an ideal n-photon outcome into a pattern with fewer photons, so the detector counts no longer follow the ideal output distribution, and the lossless events that do follow it become exponentially rare as the photon number grows. Discarding the lossy events (postselection) therefore wastes most of the data at realistic loss rates, and the ideal distribution has to be inferred from the lossy counts themselves. Recycling-based mitigation (Mills & Mezher, Quantum 2026; Quandela's photon_recycling) reweights lossy samples to recover lossless probabilities, but its estimators are biased and restricted to the no-collision sector, where each output mode holds at most one photon. We instead treat the raw counts as Multinomial observations under per-photon binomial loss and infer the ideal output distribution and the loss rate jointly from a Bayesian posterior, which extends naturally to outputs with collisions. On data from the independent Perceval simulator at the scale of prior work (n=4 photons in m=20 and m=10 modes), the posterior has lower KL divergence than both recycling and postselection at every tested loss rate in the no-collision benchmark. In the collision regime it recovers the loss rate and the collision-pattern probabilities, which recycling cannot estimate, and stays below recycling at every loss rate and below postselection except at low loss, where the two are comparable. Its advantage over recycling grows with the sample count, and it supplies credible intervals that the baselines lack.
tldr: A Bayesian inference framework is proposed to jointly estimate the lossless output distribution and the per-photon loss rate from lossy detector counts in linear optical quantum circuits, including collision regimes.
motivation: Photon loss is the dominant noise in linear optical circuits; postselecting lossless events discards most data, while existing recycling-based mitigation is biased and limited to the no-collision sector where each mode holds at most one photon.
method: Raw detector counts are modelled as Multinomial observations under per-photon binomial loss, and the ideal output distribution and loss rate are inferred jointly from a Bayesian posterior that naturally handles collision patterns with multiple photons per mode.
result: On Perceval simulator data (n=4 photons, m=20 and m=10 modes), the posterior achieves lower KL divergence than recycling and postselection at every tested loss rate in the no-collision benchmark, and in the collision regime it recovers the loss rate and collision-pattern probabilities that recycling cannot estimate, with advantages growing with sample count.
conclusion: Collision-aware Bayesian mitigation offers an unbiased, uncertainty-quantified alternative to recycling-based loss mitigation for linear optical quantum circuits, though evaluation remains simulation-based at small photon numbers.

title: Certified Adaptive List Decoding For Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Jaeho Hwang, Byung-Sun Won, Uiwon Hwang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding of linear block codes is NP-hard, so neural decoders are evaluated by how closely they approach it. We observe that proving a candidate optimal can be far easier than finding it, and build a decoder that does both. We cast decoding as a search over an absorbing-state discrete diffusion model, whose sequential commitment of coordinates turns generation into a tree, and run a probability beam search over it. A dual bound from a linear-programming relaxation and a distance-based test, both derived from the code, then certify per frame that the current candidate is the global ML solution; because both are theorems, certified frames incur no accuracy-computation trade-off. Across [MATH] codes and five operating points we certify up to [MATH] of frames, the two tests dividing the space as their derivations predict, one strong for sparse parity-check matrices and the other for codes with a large minimum distance. Certification also behaves as a per-frame reliability signal, with [MATH]-[MATH] of all frame errors falling on uncertified frames. Against an exact ML reference at [MATH] dB the decoder is within one standard deviation on three of the four codes where the reference is uncensored, and against four neural baselines it attains the best bit-error rate in [MATH] of [MATH] cells.
tldr: The paper proposes a certified adaptive list decoder for classical linear block codes, combining a diffusion-model beam search with LP-dual and distance-based certificates for maximum-likelihood optimality.
motivation: Maximum-likelihood decoding of linear block codes is NP-hard, so practical decoders are judged by proximity to ML; the authors observe that certifying optimality can be easier than finding the optimum.
