method: The authors combine a Volterra-resolvent analysis with backward Euler convolution quadrature and Fourier pseudospectral spatial discretization, then accelerate the scheme via Cauchy-FFT weight recovery and adaptive blockwise sum-of-exponentials compression of the memory history.
result: A logarithmic perturbation bound quantifies errors from weight recovery, history compression, and inexact nonlinear solves, yielding tolerance conditions that preserve first-order convergence; numerics confirm first-order accuracy and large speedups for long-time spatial patterns.
conclusion: The accelerated convolution quadrature method provides mesh-uniform stability and efficient long-time resolution of variable-order fractional reaction-diffusion dynamics at substantially reduced computational cost.

title: Soliton Profiles In 1d: Enhanced Neural-Network Solvers And Constrained Deep Ritz Methods
authors: Chandler Haight, Alex D Rodriguez, Svetlana Roudenko
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop and compare enhanced neural-network solvers for one-dimensional ground-state profiles, which are solutions of $[MATH]$ the stationary profile equation for the nonlinear Schr\"odinger, generalized Korteweg-de Vries, and nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations. Its explicit sech-type solutions serve as exact reference for error computation and benchmark hyperparameter selection. We improve on the standard Adam-trained physics-informed neural network (PINN) baseline by introducing higher-order optimization via Gauss-Newton/Levenberg-Marquardt and L-BFGS refinements, as well as Fourier-feature PINNs, and constrained Deep Ritz (DR) formulations. In DR approaches we introduce two new neural-network formulations, which implement two classical variational characterizations: a Nehari-constrained Deep Ritz method, in which the height is learned by projecting onto the Nehari/Pokhozhaev manifold, and a Weinstein Deep Ritz method, in which a normalized profile minimizes the Weinstein quotient. The Deep Ritz formulations perform best overall, in particular, the Weinstein variant gives the best error-runtime balance. The neural-network based solvers remain less accurate and efficient than classical Petviashvili iteration in 1D, however, the current study provides a proof of concept: the mesh-free formulation, non-reliance on exact profiles or the related features make them promising in higher dimensions and for more complicated nonlinearities and dispersive operators.
tldr: The paper develops and benchmarks neural-network solvers for one-dimensional soliton ground-state profiles of nonlinear Schrödinger, generalized Korteweg-de Vries, and nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations.
motivation: The authors aim to improve physics-informed neural-network approaches for stationary soliton profile equations and compare them with classical numerical solvers.
method: They enhance PINNs with Gauss-Newton/Levenberg-Marquardt and L-BFGS optimization, Fourier features, and constrained Deep Ritz formulations including Nehari- and Weinstein-based variational characterizations.
result: Deep Ritz methods perform best overall, with the Weinstein variant giving the best error-runtime balance, though all neural-network solvers remain less accurate and efficient than Petviashvili iteration in one dimension.
conclusion: The study is a proof of concept for mesh-free neural-network solvers that may be promising in higher dimensions and for more complicated nonlinearities and dispersive operators.

title: AoI-Aware Polar Code Blind Rate Adaptation
authors: Hassan Tavakoli
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study adaptive prefix-length selection for reliability-ordered coded transmission over [MATH] coordinates, using only the [MATH] most reliable, to balance age of information (AoI) against throughput. An additive-increase/decrease (AID) prefix-walk controller updates the prefix length from the last decoding outcome alone, at [MATH] per-slot cost with no channel estimation, inducing an irreducible birth--death chain whose mean drift fixes a unique balance point [MATH] (largest [MATH] with success probability [MATH]), around which the stationary distribution concentrates geometrically. We derive this distribution in closed form via detailed balance and obtain exact steady-state AoI and goodput via renewal-reward analysis. Simulations on a [MATH]-coordinate polar code over a binary symmetric channel (BSC) confirm these predictions to within [MATH]. Relative to a genie-aided upper bound with perfect channel knowledge, we further quantify the goodput cost of adapting from a single feedback bit alone.
tldr: A classical polar-code prefix-length adaptation scheme that trades age of information against goodput using a single feedback bit.
motivation: Adapting code rate without channel estimation is desirable in low-latency status-update systems where AoI matters, but only one bit of feedback is available.
method: An additive-increase/decrease prefix-walk controller on the reliability-ordered prefix of a polar code, analyzed as a birth-death chain via detailed balance and renewal-reward theory.
result: Closed-form stationary distribution, exact steady-state AoI and goodput, verified by BSC simulations to within a small tolerance, plus quantification of the goodput gap to a genie-aided bound.
conclusion: Single-bit feedback suffices for near-optimal AoI-throughput trade-offs in polar-coded transmission, with a quantifiable cost relative to perfect channel knowledge.

title: Mind Your Boundaries: Boundary-Aware Model Obfuscation Against Cross-node Attack
authors: Yuyang Zhang, Yihui Jin, Kangjie Chen, Leyang Wu, Run Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the advancement of powerful AI chips, on-device machine learning is gaining traction for its low latency and privacy protection. However, when edge devices are compromised, attackers can obtain white-box access to the deployed models by reversing the apps directly to obtain the knowledge of peer devices, which is known as Cross-Node Attacks, like performing efficient adversarial attacks. Most existing defenses target known vulnerabilities, yet white-box access still enables attackers to uncover more unknown weaknesses. This creates a critical risk for edge-device deployments, where one compromised device can endanger all models distributed from the same source. Motivated by findings that the model robustness is primarily influenced by the curvature of the decision boundary, we investigate how model parameters shape its curvature. In this paper, we propose a novel method, BMO, that obfuscates model parameters to diversify the decision boundary further resisting cross-node attack while preserving its benign accuracy. Specifically, we explore decomposing model parameters into boundary-position and boundary-curvature components based on null-space constraints, then models with differentiated decision boundaries are instantiated by injecting noise into the boundary-curvature component. Across all four major types of adversarial attacks with four widely-deployed on-device models, BMO achieves an average success rate of 68.68% in defense, far exceeding the most competitive baseline, which attains only 22.32% in defending against cross-node attacks. Moreover, BMO achieves comparable performance in benign accuracy compared with baselines.
tldr: The paper proposes BMO, a boundary-aware model obfuscation method that perturbs decision-boundary curvature components of on-device model parameters to defend against cross-node white-box adversarial attacks.
motivation: When edge devices are compromised, attackers gain white-box access to deployed models and can craft transferable adversarial examples that threaten all models distributed from the same source, and existing defenses only target known vulnerabilities.
method: The authors decompose model parameters into boundary-position and boundary-curvature components using null-space constraints, then inject noise into the curvature component to instantiate models with differentiated decision boundaries while preserving benign accuracy.
result: Across four major adversarial attack types and four widely deployed on-device models, BMO achieves an average defense success rate of 68.68%, compared with 22.32% for the strongest baseline, while maintaining comparable benign accuracy.
conclusion: Boundary-curvature-aware parameter obfuscation is an effective and accuracy-preserving defense for edge-deployed models against cross-node white-box adversarial attacks.

title: When Models Know But Can't Linearly Say: Relational Encoding Limits Linear Vulnerability Classification In Code LLMs
authors: Rui Melo, Andre Catarino, Claudia Mamede, Corina Pasareanu, Rui Abreu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can detect vulnerable code, yet the form of vulnerability encoding in their representations remains unclear. We analyze 8 code models spanning 6.7B-15B parameters on C programs using three datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE-BUGS), comparing two diagnostic tasks on the same representations: identifying what patterns the code instantiates, and determining whether it is vulnerable. Models encode the first with high fidelity. Under the studied paired C-code datasets and linear-probing setup, vulnerability information is more accessible as a paired relational signal-whether code A is riskier than code B-than as a globally separable categorical label. This structural difference has implications for classification: the model reliably ranks which code is riskier but standard classifiers on isolated samples achieve limited accuracy because vulnerable and secure samples form overlapping distributions in representation space.
tldr: An empirical study of how eight code LLMs (6.7B-15B) internally represent code vulnerability, showing that relational (pairwise) signals are far more linearly accessible than categorical vulnerability labels.
motivation: LLMs can flag vulnerable code, but it is unclear how vulnerability information is encoded in their hidden representations, which matters for building reliable classifiers and understanding model limitations.
method: Linear probing of internal representations across three C-code datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, PRECISE-BUGS), comparing a pattern-identification probe against a vulnerability probe, both as global categorical classification and as paired relational judgments (is A riskier than B).
result: Models encode code patterns with high fidelity, but vulnerability information is much better captured as a paired relational signal than as a linearly separable categorical label; vulnerable and secure samples form heavily overlapping distributions in representation space.
conclusion: Pairwise ranking of code risk is reliable while per-sample linear classification is limited, implying representation geometry—not just knowledge—constrains vulnerability detection and motivating relational or contrastive probing approaches.

title: Guided Diffusion For Trustworthy Synthetic Text Generation
authors: Qi Pang, Hanshen Xiao, Andre Manoel, Lipika Ramaswamy, Wenting Zheng, Virginia Smith, G. Edward Suh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models is fueled by massive datasets, yet this reliance poses severe privacy risks, as models can inadvertently memorize and even directly output sensitive training data. Synthetic text generation offers a promising solution to this challenge; however, existing methods struggle to reconcile rigorous privacy guarantees with high data utility. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm for private synthetic text generation: Guided Diffusion. Leveraging the unique steerability of Diffusion Language Models, we introduce novel sampling and re-masking procedures that actively guide the iterative denoising steps. These mechanisms steer the generative process to reconstruct fluent text that adheres to a target semantic distribution. We demonstrate that our framework is naturally compatible with Differential Privacy (DP): once the semantic embeddings of the private corpus are protected, the DP guarantee carries over to the generated text by post-processing. Empirically, we show that our approach generates high-quality synthetic text with precise semantic alignment. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness in DP synthetic text generation: across two datasets and two diffusion backbones, it outperforms Private Evolution and DP-SGD-based fine-tuning in distributional fidelity and downstream utility, while generating significantly faster than Private Evolution. We further extend the framework to Data-Specific Indistinguishability (DSI), which adds a formal certificate against data poisoning and memorization at a small utility cost.
tldr: The paper proposes Guided Diffusion, a framework for differentially private synthetic text generation that steers diffusion language models toward a target semantic distribution via novel sampling and re-masking procedures.
motivation: Large language models risk memorizing and leaking sensitive training data, and existing private synthetic text generation methods struggle to combine rigorous privacy guarantees with high utility.
method: The authors exploit the steerability of diffusion language models, adding guided sampling and re-masking steps so that denoising reconstructs fluent text matching a target semantic distribution; protecting semantic embeddings of the private corpus makes generated text differentially private by post-processing.
result: Across two datasets and two diffusion backbones, the method outperforms Private Evolution and DP-SGD-based fine-tuning in distributional fidelity and downstream utility while generating much faster; an extension to Data-Specific Indistinguishability is also demonstrated.
conclusion: Guided diffusion offers a practical, trustworthy paradigm for private synthetic text generation, though at a small utility cost under the stronger DSI certification.

title: Privacy-Preserving Personalized Federated Learning (ppp-fl) For Medical Imaging
authors: Md Morshedul Islam, Hossain Shahriar, Alfredo Cuzzocrea
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that reduces transmission costs, mitigates cross-border data sharing restrictions, and enhances privacy by keeping raw data on local devices. Clients in FL systems train local models and share only updates, which are aggregated by a central server. While this setup limits direct data exposure, FL remains vulnerable to privacy attacks. Existing attack and defense strategies have largely been developed for centralized systems, and adapting them to FL introduces new challenges due to its unique architecture and training workflow. In this work, we first propose a model inversion attack on FL systems using Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) in the context of large-scale medical imaging. Our method operates under realistic assumptions about the attacker's knowledge and capabilities. We then examine the effect of client-side differential privacy (DP) in mitigating privacy leakage and incorporate personalized FL to improve model performance under DP settings. Experiments on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset show that DCGAN-based attacks can reconstruct semantically meaningful synthetic images, revealing significant risks to the privacy of training data. Applying DP reduces attack success but introduces an accuracy trade-off, which is further overcome by personalized FL at each client side. We also evaluate how different aggregation algorithms affect both attack vulnerability and defense effectiveness, underscoring the critical role of aggregation strategies. The proposed attack-and-defense framework is model-agnostic and applicable to a wide range of FL-based systems.
tldr: The paper proposes a DCGAN-based model inversion attack against federated learning for medical imaging and evaluates client-side differential privacy plus personalized FL as defenses.
motivation: Federated learning is widely assumed to protect privacy by keeping data local, but gradient/model updates can leak training data; existing attack and defense analyses are mostly designed for centralized settings.
method: A DCGAN-based model inversion attack is developed under realistic attacker assumptions on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset, then client-side differential privacy and personalized FL are tested as mitigations across several aggregation algorithms.
result: The attack reconstructs semantically meaningful synthetic MRI images, showing substantial privacy leakage; differential privacy reduces attack success at the cost of accuracy, and personalized FL partially recovers the lost accuracy.
conclusion: Aggregation strategy strongly influences both vulnerability and defense effectiveness, and the model-agnostic attack-and-defense framework is claimed applicable to general FL systems.

title: Commutative Coarse-graining On The Sphere
authors: Hussein Aluie Chayut Teeraratkul
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. We discuss the root of the problem, which is intrinsic to the curved geometry rather than being a result of metric terms, coordinate system, or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.
tldr: The paper develops a curvature-aware spherical convolution that commutes with differential operators for consistent coarse-graining on the sphere.
motivation: Standard spatial filtering on the sphere fails to commute with divergence, curl, and radial projection, producing spurious gradients and divergences in coarse-grained dynamics.
method: The authors identify the geometric origin of the non-commutation and show that a generalized spherical convolution is the unique linear operator commuting with radial projection, divergence, and curl for a given scalar kernel.
result: In simulations of an unstable jet, the generalized convolution commutes to numerical round-off, while conventional filtering ignoring curvature yields significant spurious divergence and gradient errors.
conclusion: Consistent coarse-graining on the sphere requires curvature-aware convolution; spectral truncation, wavelets, diffusion, and learned convolutions must all take this generalized form to preserve physics across scales.

title: Enhancing Analytical Photon Transport In Turbid Media Through Physics-guided Neural Network Corrections
authors: Guojun Tang, Paul D. Teal, Alexander Doronin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analytical methods provide rapid and computationally efficient predictions of light transport in turbid media, making them attractive for real-time and inverse applications. However, their accuracy is limited by the approximations and assumptions used to obtain tractable solutions. On the other hand, Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is widely regarded as the "gold standard" for modeling light transport in turbid media, but its high computational cost limits its use in applications requiring repeated forward evaluations. Here, we introduce a physics-guided residual learning framework that combines the computational efficiency of analytical modeling with the accuracy of MC simulation. As a representative case study, we consider the diffusion approximation (DA), which can exhibit systematic errors under relatively strong absorption, weak scattering, and imperfect boundary treatment. Given the absorption coefficient, scattering coefficient, and anisotropy factor, the corresponding DA prediction is incorporated as a physical prior, while the network learns only the residual between the analytical prediction and the MC reference. Across the evaluated optical-property range, the proposed framework reduces scalar-reflectance RMSE and spatially resolved reflectance RMSLE by factors of approximately 62 and 14, respectively, relative to the diffusion approximation. With only 1\% of the available training data, it achieves approximately 87\% and 93\% lower corresponding errors than a direct neural-network surrogate. These results demonstrate that learning corrections to an analytical physical baseline improves both prediction accuracy and data efficiency.
tldr: A physics-guided residual neural network learns corrections to the diffusion approximation, dramatically improving accuracy and data efficiency for modeling light transport in turbid media.
motivation: Analytical light-transport models like the diffusion approximation are fast but inaccurate under strong absorption or weak scattering, while Monte Carlo simulation is accurate but computationally expensive for repeated forward evaluations.
method: The authors use the diffusion-approximation prediction as a physical prior and train a neural network to learn only the residual between this analytical prediction and Monte Carlo reference data.
result: The framework reduces scalar-reflectance RMSE and spatially resolved reflectance RMSLE by factors of ~62 and ~14 versus the diffusion approximation, and with only 1% of training data achieves ~87% and ~93% lower errors than a direct neural-network surrogate.
conclusion: Learning corrections to an analytical physical baseline improves both prediction accuracy and data efficiency, making real-time and inverse light-transport applications more feasible.

title: A Geometric Principle For Path Selection In Directed Acyclic Graphs
authors: Tim S. Evans Haya Almuhanna
abstract:
ArXiv:2610.27025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There are many types of path between nodes of a Directed acyclic graph (DAG), including the shortest and longest paths. Here, we ask whether the choice of path used in any analysis reflects the geometry of the latent space in which the DAG is embedded. To do this we define L_p-cube spacetimes, a family of continuous ordered spaces in which a single parameter p determines whether the ordered distance satisfies the ordered triangle identity when p>1, or the reverse ordered triangle identity when 0

<1 or p<0, both of which are rarely studied. The forward connection kernel in the p<0 case has infinite hyper-volume, yet it is a well defined model. We then construct random geometric DAGs embedded in our L_p-cube spacetime and study their geometry. For p>1, where the ordered triangle identity holds, the shortest paths provide the closest approximation to the continuum ordered geodesic while for 0

<1 and p<0, where the reverse ordered triangle identity holds, this role is instead taken by the longest weighted path. We also test the robustness of this relationship in a geometric citation model in which the random geometric DAG is supplemented by a preferential-attachment-type mechanism allowing connections beyond the strict geometric cut-off. The same broad correspondence between latent geometry and ordered geodesic path type is recovered. Our results show that the preference for shortest or longest paths in a DAG is closely connected to the geometry assumed for its latent space, and suggest that path structure can provide information about latent geometry, even when that geometry is not directly observed.
tldr: The paper proposes a geometric principle explaining whether shortest or longest paths in a directed acyclic graph best approximate latent-space geodesics, using a family of L_p-cube spacetimes.
motivation: Path-based analyses of DAGs (shortest vs. longest paths) are ubiquitous, but it is unclear whether the chosen path type reflects any underlying latent geometry of the graph.
method: The authors define L_p-cube spacetimes with a parameter p controlling whether an ordered triangle identity or its reverse holds, construct random geometric DAGs in these spaces, and test robustness with a preferential-attachment citation model.
result: For p>1 shortest paths best approximate the continuum ordered geodesic, while for 0<p<1 and p<0 the longest weighted path plays this role; the correspondence survives added preferential attachment.
conclusion: Preference for shortest versus longest paths encodes information about the latent geometry of a DAG, allowing path structure to be used to infer unobserved geometry.

title: Analytical Solution Of Electromagnetic Heating In A Stratified Absorbing Medium
authors: Hongyun Wang Ulises Jaime-Yepez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the temperature evolution in a skin tissue when it is exposed to an electromagnetic wave. The heating is caused by the absorbed power as the electromagnetic wave attenuates inside the skin. In many applications, the characteristic depth of attenuation is small in comparison with the lateral size of the electromagnetic beam. Because of this separation of length scales, the lateral heat conduction is negligible at leading order. Previously, we studied electromagnetic heating in a skin of a single homogeneous layer. We derived the leading-term analytical solution and the asymptotic corrections up to the second order for lateral heat conduction and for oblique incidence. In this study, we derive the analytical solution in the case of perpendicular incidence on a stratified skin tissue with a layer-specific profile for electromagnetic attenuation. It should be emphasized that in the current study, the heat capacity and conductivity are still uniform over the entire skin tissue; only the electromagnetic attenuation is stratified resulting in a layer-specific heating profile.
tldr: The paper derives analytical solutions for temperature evolution in stratified skin tissue heated by an electromagnetic wave under perpendicular incidence.
motivation: Electromagnetic heating in biological tissue is relevant to medical and safety applications, and prior work treated homogeneous single-layer skin; stratified attenuation profiles require a more general analytical treatment.
method: The authors solve the heat equation with negligible lateral conduction at leading order for perpendicular incidence, incorporating layer-specific electromagnetic attenuation while keeping heat capacity and conductivity uniform.
result: An analytical solution is obtained for the temperature profile in a stratified absorbing medium, extending earlier homogeneous-layer results to layered attenuation profiles.
conclusion: The work provides a tractable analytical model for electromagnetic heating in stratified tissue, useful when attenuation depth is small compared with beam size.

title: Machine-learned Spectral Pde Solvers For Fluids And Plasmas
authors: Alan A. Kaptanoglu Mellow Baixuan Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse regression methods for discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from data are sensitive to observation noise and are not constrained to reproduce the data under forward integration. We address both limitations by performing weak-form discovery in the spatial discretization in which the PDE is solved, learned by differentiating through multistep rollouts anchored at the observed states. The new method, Weak-form Anchored Rollout for PDEs (WARP), produces a machine-learned PDE solver. In this work, we focus on systems amenable to a spectral Galerkin solver. Across eight benchmark fluid and plasma systems, including high-dimensional turbulent simulations, WARP produces numerically stable rollouts from new random initial conditions and substantially improves coefficient recovery, rollout accuracy, and statistical measures compared with a single-step weak-form SINDy baseline.
tldr: WARP, a weak-form sparse-regression method that learns spectral Galerkin PDE solvers by differentiating through multistep rollouts anchored at observed states, improves coefficient recovery and rollout stability for fluid and plasma systems.
motivation: Sparse regression PDE discovery (SINDy) is fragile under observation noise and does not guarantee that the recovered model reproduces data under forward integration, so the authors seek a discovery scheme that is both noise-robust and rollout-consistent.
method: They perform weak-form equation discovery directly in the spatial discretization used for solving, training via backpropagation through multistep spectral Galerkin rollouts anchored at observed states, yielding a machine-learned PDE solver.
result: Across eight benchmark fluid and plasma systems, including high-dimensional turbulent simulations, WARP gives numerically stable rollouts from new random initial conditions and substantially better coefficient recovery, rollout accuracy, and statistical measures than a single-step weak-form SINDy baseline.
conclusion: Anchoring weak-form discovery to multistep differentiable rollouts yields more reliable, physically consistent learned PDE models for spectral solvers, with benefits for turbulent and high-dimensional plasma/fluid dynamics.

title: Lucas Recurrences And Lambert Series In Coprime Double Sums
authors: Nikita Kalinin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the Lucas numbers [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], we obtain \[ \sum_{}{L_{2n}L_{2m}L_{2(n+m)}}=\frac1{45}. \] This follows from the absolutely convergent identity \[ \sum_{}} {(1+q^n)(1+q^m)(1+q^{n+m})} ={(1-q^2)^2},\qquad |q|<1. \] We give a self-contained proof by local cancellation on the Calkin--Wilf tree, as a specialization of Hata's Farey-interval telescoping principle. Specializations yield a hyperbolic-cosine identity \[\sum_{} {\cosh(nx)\cosh(mx)\cosh((n+m)x)} ={\sinh^2(2x)}, x>0\] and weighted sums for canonical second-order Lucas recurrences. Decomposing arbitrary positive pairs according to their greatest common divisor gives an unrestricted sum expressed by a Lambert series and the quasimodular Eisenstein series [MATH]. Conversely, M\"obius inversion recovers the primitive identity from a double Lambert-series result of Cui, Kumar, and Singh.
tldr: The paper derives closed-form evaluations of coprime-restricted double sums involving Lucas numbers via a local-cancellation proof on the Calkin–Wilf tree, together with Lambert-series and Eisenstein-series generalizations.
motivation: The authors aim to evaluate certain double sums over coprime indices of products of Lucas numbers and hyperbolic cosines, extending Hata's Farey-interval telescoping principle to new settings.
method: A self-contained proof by local cancellation on the Calkin–Wilf tree is used, together with gcd-decomposition of positive integer pairs, Lambert series, the quasimodular Eisenstein series, and Möbius inversion.
result: They obtain identities such as a sum of Lucas products equal to 1/45, an absolutely convergent q-series identity, a hyperbolic-cosine specialization, and a Lambert-series representation of the unrestricted sum.
conclusion: The work connects coprime double sums to Lambert series and quasimodular forms, and shows that Möbius inversion recovers a primitive identity from a known double Lambert-series result.

title: Iterated Lavrentiev Regularization Under Random Noise: Variational Source Conditions And Rates In Expectation
authors: Ankit Singh, Hemant Sharma, Kiran Davuluri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The convergence theory of iterated Lavrentiev regularization for nonlinear monotone ill-posed equations is deterministic: the data error is bounded by a known level that the discrepancy principle uses explicitly. Under Gaussian noise no such bound exists. For a discretized two-dimensional nonlinear inverse source problem for the Poisson equation, we analyse convergence in a finite-energy Gaussian noise model, keeping the linearized and nonlinear cases apart. For the linearized iteration the noisy and noise-free iterates differ by one resolvent applied to the noise; this gives an exact singular-value variance formula, a priori rates in expectation, and the main result: for a family of discretizations whose distance functions are bounded uniformly in the mesh, the rate is governed by that decay, which relaxes the classical range condition. The rate degrades gracefully, down to logarithmic, as the underlying continuum error loses smoothness, and a balancing rule attains it without knowing the smoothness. For the full nonlinear iteration under the order-one source condition, a truncated discrepancy principle fed only the noise level attains [MATH] in expectation, in the energy noise level [MATH], the rare event of large noise being controlled by concentration. The rough nonlinear regime and the general-exponent nonlinear rate are left open and supported numerically for kink and jump errors. We separate the deterministic worst-case, Gaussian, and white-noise settings, prove a worst-case lower bound, and describe where the method is statistically inefficient relative to spectral cut-off. Heterogeneous media and a cost comparison with an adjoint-based scheme are given as supplementary material.
tldr: The paper analyzes convergence rates in expectation for iterated Lavrentiev regularization of nonlinear monotone ill-posed equations under Gaussian noise, applied to a discretized 2D inverse source problem for the Poisson equation.
motivation: Classical convergence theory for iterated Lavrentiev regularization assumes a deterministic noise bound usable in the discrepancy principle; Gaussian noise violates this assumption, so a stochastic-noise convergence theory is needed.
method: Separating linearized and nonlinear iterations, the authors derive an exact singular-value variance formula for the linearized case, prove a priori rates in expectation governed by the decay of discretization distance functions, and use a truncated discrepancy principle with concentration arguments for the nonlinear case under an order-one source condition.
result: Rates in expectation are obtained that relax the classical range condition, degrade gracefully (down to logarithmic) as smoothness is lost, and are attained by a balancing rule without knowledge of smoothness; a worst-case lower bound separates deterministic, Gaussian, and white-noise settings.
conclusion: The work extends regularization theory to stochastic noise regimes, identifies regimes where the method is statistically inefficient compared with spectral cut-off, and leaves the rough nonlinear regime and general-exponent rates open, supported numerically.

title: A 2x2 Matrix Approach To Hopf Fibrations:: Quaternionic Reduction Of Octonionic Bi-unitary Matrices And An Rllr/lrrl Bracketing Rule
authors: Aneta Sli\.{z}ewska Jean-Pierre Gazeau
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a common two-by-two matrix framework for the four classical Hopf fibrations associated with the real, complex, quaternionic and octonionic numbers. In all four cases the Hopf map is the image of the north pole of a sphere of trace-free Hermitian matrices under conjugation by a bi-unitary matrix, and it depends only on the first column of that matrix, without any bracketing convention, even for the non-associative octonions. Our main results concern general octonionic bi-unitary matrices, beyond the compatible matrices, with entries in a single complex subalgebra, on which earlier work on octonionic Lorentz transformations relies. We prove that every octonionic bi-unitary matrix is in fact quaternionic: its entries lie in a quaternion subalgebra depending on the matrix. We show that requiring Hermitian output leaves exactly four inequivalent ways of bracketing the octonionic triple products, among them an interlaced rule called RLLR/LRRL, and that each of them splits into an ordinary five-dimensional rotation and a four-dimensional scaling governed by a non-commutative determinant. This determines exactly when the evaluation preserves the geometry of the sphere, shows that it may contract or even collapse four dimensions, and explains why it cannot be compatible with matrix multiplication. We also recover in compact form, through the Clifford map, the known fact that suitable compatible matrices, which we interpret as transvections of the eight-sphere, generate the spin group Spin(9) by nested evaluations. Non-associativity thus does not prevent a two-by-two octonionic description of the full Spin(9) symmetry; it prevents that description from being realised through unrestricted multiplication of octonionic matrices.
tldr: This is a pure mathematical paper on a unified 2x2 matrix description of Hopf fibrations, with a focus on octonionic bi-unitary matrices and Spin(9).
motivation: The authors aim to provide a common framework for real, complex, quaternionic, and octonionic Hopf fibrations and to analyze non-associative octonionic matrix structures beyond compatible matrices.
method: They represent Hopf maps via conjugation of trace-free Hermitian matrices by bi-unitary matrices and classify bracketing rules for octonionic triple products under Hermiticity constraints.
result: They prove every octonionic bi-unitary matrix is quaternionic, identify four inequivalent bracketing rules including RLLR/LRRL, and show how these split into a five-dimensional rotation and four-dimensional scaling.
conclusion: The paper clarifies structural limitations of octonionic matrix multiplication while recovering Spin(9) symmetry through compatible matrices, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Convex-cyclic And Super Convex-cyclic Weighted Shifts
authors: Ze-Hua Zhou Cui Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Convex-cyclic operators are considered by H. Rezaei . However, there is a general lack of theoretical understanding of super convex-cyclic operators. In this paper, we analyze super convex-cyclic operators. In particular, Super Convex-cyclicity Criterion is described. Additionally, we characterize convex-cyclicity of (invertible) bilateral weighted shifts in terms of their weight sequences, which in turn correct \cite[H. Rezaei (2013) Theorem 4.2 ]{R1}. Meanwhile, we give super convex-cyclicity of (invertible) weighted shifts in the bilateral case.
tldr: The paper studies super convex-cyclic operators and characterizes convex-cyclicity of bilateral weighted shifts via their weight sequences, correcting an earlier theorem by Rezaei.
motivation: Convex-cyclic operators have been previously considered, but super convex-cyclic operators lack theoretical understanding, prompting a systematic analysis of this notion.
method: The authors establish a Super Convex-cyclicity Criterion and analyze convex-cyclicity and super convex-cyclicity of invertible bilateral weighted shifts in terms of their weight sequences.
result: They provide a corrected characterization of convex-cyclicity for bilateral weighted shifts, refining Rezaei's Theorem 4.2, and give conditions for super convex-cyclicity in the bilateral case.
conclusion: The work clarifies the theory of (super) convex-cyclic operators and extends cyclicity criteria to weighted shift operators, but remains within pure operator theory.

title: Euler Time-Discretization Of Funnel-Controlled Dynamics
authors: Thomas Berger, Hannes Gernandt, Pushya Mitra
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze explicit and implicit Euler discretizations of the continuous-time closed-loop dynamics generated by a funnel controller for a fully actuated nonlinear full-state system of relative degree one with scalar positive input gain. A quantitative continuous-time funnel margin provides the compactness and regularity bounds needed for the error analysis. For explicit Euler, a computable upper step-size threshold guarantees a global nodewise distance from the funnel boundary. We show that first-order convergence holds on finite time horizons and, under a~dissipativity condition (a~one-sided Lipschitz bound on the plant dominated by the funnel damping), uniformly in time. For implicit Euler, an admissible update exists for every step size and every trajectory initialized in the funnel retains a step-size-independent nodal margin. Under dissipativity, the admissible root is unique for every step size, the discrete flow is contractive, and the first-order error bound is uniform in time.
tldr: The paper analyzes explicit and implicit Euler discretizations of continuous-time funnel-controlled nonlinear plant dynamics, proving first-order convergence and step-size-independent margin guarantees.
motivation: Funnel control enforces prescribed transient and steady-state performance for uncertain nonlinear systems, but practical implementation requires digital (discrete-time) updates, so a rigorous discrete-time error analysis is needed.
method: Using a quantitative continuous-time funnel margin to obtain compactness and regularity bounds, the authors derive step-size thresholds for explicit Euler and prove existence, uniqueness, and contractivity of the implicit Euler update under a dissipativity (one-sided Lipschitz) condition.
result: Explicit Euler achieves global nodewise distance from the funnel boundary with a computable step-size bound and first-order convergence, uniform in time under dissipativity; implicit Euler admits an admissible root for every step size with a step-size-independent nodal margin and contractive discrete flow.
conclusion: Funnel-controlled dynamics can be reliably discretized while preserving performance guarantees, with implicit Euler offering stronger robustness properties at the cost of solving a root equation.

title: Combining Exponential And Polynomial Convergence Rates For Accelerated Extremum Seeking: A High-Order Lie Bracket Approach
authors: Sameh Eisa Victoria Grushkovskaya
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we leverage the recently developed general higher-order Lie bracket approximation theory and framework for control-affine systems to show that we can design extremum seeking (ES) systems that combine flows based on: (i) first-order Lie bracket approximation, which provide an exponential convergence rate for quadratic objective functions and polynomial convergence rate for non-quadratic objective functions; and (ii) higher-order Lie bracket approximation, which provide exponential convergence rate near the minimizer even if the objective function is non-quadratic (i.e., flatter and possesses vanishing Hessian at the minimizer). Such combination provides an accelerated ES design that benefits from the polynomial decay rate farther away from the minimizer and exponential decay rate near the minimizer even for complicated nature of objective functions. We provide numerical simulations to demonstrate the results, including multi-variable and nonpolynomial flat-bottomed objective functions.
tldr: The paper designs accelerated extremum-seeking controllers by combining first-order and higher-order Lie bracket approximations to achieve polynomial convergence far from the optimum and exponential convergence near it.
motivation: Standard extremum-seeking schemes may converge slowly or fail to achieve exponential rates for non-quadratic objectives, especially flat-bottomed functions with vanishing Hessian at the minimizer.
method: Using higher-order Lie bracket approximation theory for control-affine systems, the authors combine flows from first-order and higher-order Lie bracket approximations into a hybrid accelerated extremum-seeking design.
result: Numerical simulations demonstrate improved convergence for multi-variable and nonpolynomial flat-bottomed objective functions, with polynomial decay away from the minimizer and exponential decay near it.
conclusion: The combined Lie bracket approach provides an accelerated extremum-seeking framework that handles challenging non-quadratic objective landscapes more effectively than either approximation alone.

title: Michael Rabin's Fingerprints Across The Theory Of Computation
authors: Avi Wigderson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Michael O. Rabin was a major founder and leader of theoretical computer science. He died on April 14, 2026, at the age of 94. This paper aims to survey the wide scope and lasting impact of his research.
tldr: A survey of Michael O. Rabin's wide-ranging and lasting contributions to theoretical computer science, written as a memorial retrospective.
motivation: Rabin, who died in April 2026 at age 94, was a founder of theoretical computer science, and the author aims to document the scope and impact of his research.
method: Historical and conceptual survey of Rabin's body of work, tracing its influence across the theory of computation rather than presenting new technical results.
result: The paper catalogues Rabin's key results and their downstream influence on theoretical computer science as a whole.
conclusion: Rabin's fingerprints are pervasive across theoretical computer science; the survey serves as a memorial and historical overview rather than a contribution to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Optimal Two-Mode Switching With Setup Costs For A Controlled Ornstein--Uhlenbeck Process
authors: Dacheng Yao Hongkun Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an infinite-horizon discounted optimal switching problem for an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process whose mean-reversion level can be switched between two values. Switching incurs positive, potentially asymmetric fixed costs, and the mode with the higher mean-reversion level entails an additional running cost. The revenue rate is proportional to the positive part of the state. We characterize the value function and identify parameter conditions under which an optimal policy either remains permanently in one mode after a possible costly initial switch or follows a threshold rule. The threshold formulation allows infinite boundaries and therefore includes one-way switching. A key technical contribution is to establish existence and uniqueness of the relevant solutions to the coupled nonlinear free-boundary equations arising from value-matching and smooth-fit conditions. In the corresponding parameter regimes, these solutions determine the finite switching thresholds and the coefficients of the candidate value functions. A verification argument then establishes the optimality of the resulting policies over all admissible switching strategies.
tldr: The paper solves an infinite-horizon optimal switching problem for a two-mode controlled Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with fixed switching costs and characterizes threshold-type optimal policies.
motivation: The authors are motivated by optimal switching control problems with mean-reverting dynamics and asymmetric setup costs, where the optimal policy may involve either permanent mode choice or threshold-based switching.
method: They formulate the problem as a discounted optimal switching problem, derive coupled nonlinear free-boundary equations from value-matching and smooth-fit conditions, and prove existence and uniqueness of solutions in relevant parameter regimes.
result: The value function is characterized, and parameter conditions are identified under which the optimal policy is either permanent mode selection after an initial switch or a threshold rule allowing infinite boundaries and one-way switching.
conclusion: A verification argument establishes optimality of the proposed policies among all admissible switching strategies, providing a rigorous solution to the controlled Ornstein-Uhlenbeck switching problem.

title: Adaptive Normalized Gradient Method For $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth Problems: Estimating Problem Parameters As A Region
authors: Rikiya Okazaki, Shotaro Yagishita, Hideitsu Hino
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a parameter-free and efficient gradient descent algorithm for [MATH]-smooth optimization. This notion of smoothness, introduced by Zhang et al. (2020), allows the smoothness bound to grow with the gradient norm. Similar to cutting-plane localization, our method uses a sequence of observations to maintain a region of plausible values for [MATH] and uses this region to select step sizes. In the convex setting, our method attains the standard iteration complexity bound [MATH] for finding an [MATH]-optimal solution, while in the nonconvex setting it finds an [MATH]-stationary point within [MATH] iterations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to establish, for a single parameter-free algorithm, the best-known iteration-complexity guarantee in the nonconvex setting while also providing the above iteration-complexity guarantee in the convex setting. Experiments on logistic regression and real phase retrieval demonstrate that our method can exploit [MATH]-smoothness and perform efficiently on nonconvex problems.
tldr: The paper proposes a parameter-free gradient descent algorithm for (L0,L1)-smooth optimization that adaptively estimates the problem's smoothness parameters by maintaining a region of plausible values, similar to cutting-plane localization.
motivation: Standard gradient descent requires knowledge of the smoothness constant to set step sizes, but in (L0,L1)-smooth problems the smoothness bound grows with the gradient norm, making parameter tuning difficult; the authors aim for a fully parameter-free method with strong complexity guarantees.
method: The algorithm maintains a shrinking region of plausible (L0,L1) parameter values based on observed gradients, and uses this region to select step sizes adaptively, drawing on cutting-plane localization ideas.
result: In the convex setting the method achieves the standard O(1/epsilon) iteration complexity for an epsilon-optimal solution, and in the nonconvex setting it finds an epsilon-stationary point within the best-known iteration bound, the first single parameter-free algorithm to achieve both; experiments on logistic regression and phase retrieval confirm efficiency.
conclusion: Adaptive region-based estimation of smoothness parameters yields a practical, parameter-free optimizer with state-of-the-art theoretical guarantees in both convex and nonconvex regimes.

title: Forest Characterization Of When Sdp-rlt Strengthens Rlt For Bilinear Terms
authors: Hayato Watanabe, Takami Sato, Kazuhide Nakata, Ken Kobayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study two relaxations for bilinear terms in box-constrained variables: the reformulation-linearization technique (RLT) relaxation and the SDP-RLT relaxation, which combines RLT with semidefinite programming (SDP). We represent the pattern of bilinear terms by an undirected graph, with one vertex for each variable and one edge for each bilinear term. A point feasible for the RLT relaxation fixes only part of the lifted matrix of the SDP-RLT relaxation, leaving the remaining entries to be chosen subject to the diagonal RLT inequalities, and the two relaxations differ exactly when these entries cannot always be chosen so that the matrix becomes positive semidefinite. Formulating this as a positive semidefinite matrix completion problem, we show that the feasible regions of the two relaxations coincide if and only if the graph is a forest. We also measure how large the difference can be when the graph contains a complete bipartite subgraph: a bilinear objective given by a Hadamard matrix yields optimal values whose ratio grows with the size of that subgraph.
tldr: The paper gives a graph-theoretic characterization (forests) of exactly when the SDP-RLT relaxation strictly strengthens the RLT relaxation for bilinear terms in box-constrained optimization.
motivation: RLT and SDP-RLT are both used to relax bilinear terms, but it was unclear when the semidefinite version provides a genuine improvement over plain RLT.
method: The pattern of bilinear terms is encoded as a graph, and the question of whether the lifted matrix can be completed to a PSD matrix subject to diagonal RLT inequalities is formulated as a PSD matrix completion problem.
result: The feasible regions of the two relaxations coincide if and only if the graph is a forest; when a complete bipartite subgraph exists, Hadamard-matrix objectives produce optimal-value ratios growing with the subgraph size.
conclusion: The work precisely delineates the structural conditions under which SDP relaxation adds value, giving both an exact characterization and a quantitative bound on the potential gap.

title: Control Variates For Dry Friction Under Colored Noise: Variance Rates For Non-smooth Observables
authors: Lihong Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A control variate method was introduced by Garnier and Mertz (2022) for multivalued stochastic differential equations driven by colored noise. For smooth observables, the asymptotic variance is [MATH], where [MATH] is the correlation time of the noise. However, for non-smooth reliability observables, such as threshold indicators and overshoot severities, rate estimates have not been established in general. In this paper, rate estimates are derived for the inertial dry-friction inclusion driven by colored noise in the three regimes whose white-noise propagators are known. The asymptotic variance of the resulting control variate estimators is [MATH] for [MATH]-H\"older observables with [MATH], [MATH] for observables of bounded variation satisfying a one-sided continuity condition, [MATH] for observables that are both [MATH]-H\"older and of bounded variation, and [MATH] for observables with finitely many [MATH]-cusps, where [MATH] is the cusp exponent. The last three bounds hold up to logarithmic factors. Bounds on the bias of the white-noise approximation and non-asymptotic sample-size estimates are also derived, and the comparison principle is shown to be preserved under coupled time discretization. Numerical experiments in the three regimes support the predicted rates.
tldr: The paper derives asymptotic variance rate estimates for control variate estimators applied to multivalued stochastic differential equations modeling dry friction under colored noise, with non-smooth observables.
motivation: Prior control variate results for colored-noise-driven multivalued SDEs only covered smooth observables, leaving non-smooth reliability observables such as threshold indicators and overshoot severities without rate estimates.
method: The authors analyze the inertial dry-friction inclusion driven by colored noise in three regimes with known white-noise propagators, deriving variance rates for Hölder, bounded-variation, and cusped observables alongside bias bounds and non-asymptotic sample-size estimates.
result: They obtain variance rates of the form dependent on the correlation time for different observable classes, up to logarithmic factors in several cases, and confirm the predicted rates via numerical experiments.
conclusion: The work extends control variate theory to non-smooth observables in dry-friction stochastic systems and provides practical bias and sample-size bounds, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: k-Submodular Cover Problem With A Matroid Constraint
authors: Xinru Li, Donglei Du, Qian Liu, Yang Zhou, Min Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate k-submodular cover problem with a matroid constraint on an n-element ground set V , which seeks k disjoint subsets of V with minimal cost, where their union is an independent set for some matroid defined on V and the k-submodular utility function surpasses a specified threshold. This problem generalizes the k-submodular cover problem and has a wide range of applications in artificial intelligence and combinatorial optimization. In this paper, we propose a matroid extended greedy algorithm for this problem, analyze its bi-criteria approximation ratio, and further derive an improved approximation ratio under the special case of unit costs.
tldr: The paper studies the k-submodular cover problem under a matroid constraint and gives a matroid-extended greedy algorithm with bi-criteria approximation guarantees, plus an improved ratio for unit costs.
motivation: The k-submodular cover problem generalizes classical submodular cover and has applications in AI and combinatorial optimization, but existing work does not handle an additional matroid independence constraint on the union of the k disjoint subsets.
method: The authors design a matroid-extended greedy algorithm that jointly selects k disjoint subsets whose union is independent in a matroid while maximizing a k-submodular utility, and they analyze its bi-criteria approximation ratio, refining it for the unit-cost case.
result: The algorithm achieves a provable bi-criteria approximation ratio, and a tighter approximation guarantee is derived under unit costs.
conclusion: The work extends submodular covering theory with matroid constraints and provides approximation guarantees, but it is a purely classical combinatorial optimization result with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Reliable Estimation Of Differential Privacy Under Selection Bias
authors: Valentin Dorseuil (di-Ens), Meenatchi Sundaram Muthu Selva Annamalai (UCL), Jamal Atif (CMAP), Olivier Capp\'e (di-Ens), Nicolas Papernot
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistical privacy audits are essential for verifying the theoretical privacy guarantees of differentially private (DP) mechanisms. Auditors typically use Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) to estimate a lower bound on the true privacy leakage of DP mechanisms at a specified confidence level, which should not exceed the theoretical privacy upper bound guaranteed by DP. However, we found that many auditing implementations in prior work introduce a selection bias when running MIAs, which leads to statistically invalid and overestimated lower bounds. Because most audits are not tight, this bias has thus far gone unnoticed: the estimated lower bounds remained well below the theoretical upper bounds. Nevertheless, accurately evaluating this lower bound is critical, as a flawed statistical assessment could lead to false alarms on correct mechanisms or an incorrect evaluation of the guarantee's tightness. This work employs tools from the statistical literature to correct this bias. We present an overview of the different correction methods and assess their respective advantages. Furthermore, we perform a comprehensive re-analysis of results returned by prior audit implementations and show that without statistical correction, these audits violate the theoretical upper bounds up to four times more often than their claimed confidence level implies. With correction applied, the resulting lower bounds are statistically valid, and violations occur at no more than the nominal rate.
tldr: The paper identifies and corrects a selection bias in statistical privacy audits of differentially private mechanisms, showing that prior membership-inference-based lower bounds were statistically invalid.
motivation: Privacy audits using membership inference attacks are meant to certify lower bounds on leakage without exceeding the theoretical DP upper bound, but auditing implementations were silently introducing selection bias that inflated these bounds.
method: The authors import bias-correction tools from the statistics literature, compare several correction approaches, and re-analyze published audit results from prior work under the corrected estimators.
result: Uncorrected audits violate the theoretical upper bounds up to four times more often than their claimed confidence level, while corrected lower bounds are statistically valid and violate at no more than the nominal rate.
conclusion: Selection bias must be statistically corrected for DP audits to be trustworthy; the proposed corrections yield valid confidence guarantees and more accurate assessments of DP tightness.

title: Echo: Revealing Review-to-Submission Linkage In Anonymous Peer Review
authors: Mulong Luo Rong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anonymous peer review protects reviewers from retaliation, yet reviewer anonymity may also be weakened by artifacts released through the review process itself. This risk is growing as many venues require submitting authors to review, creating substantial overlap between authors and reviewers within the same review cycle. We identify review-to-submission linkage, where an anonymous review can be associated with the reviewer's own submission, substantially shrinking the reviewer anonymity set. To assess whether this linkage is practically exploitable, we develop ECHO, which combines technical-expertise and writing-style signals across reviews, papers, and rebuttals, and evaluate it on R2S-Bench, a ground-truth benchmark we construct. ECHO correctly identifies the reviewer's own submission in Top-1 for 34.6% of reviews, in the Top-5 for 54.0%, and in the Top-10 for 63.4%, compared with 0.5%, 2.6%, and 5.3% under random ranking, from the candidate submissions. With a stronger Stage-2 reranker, ECHO further reaches 56.4% Top-1 and 66.4% Top-10. These results demonstrate that review-to-submission linkage is feasible using only routinely released peer-review artifacts. Code and benchmark are available at [URL].
tldr: The paper identifies and demonstrates review-to-submission linkage in anonymous peer review, where an anonymous review can be matched to the reviewer's own submission using routinely released artifacts.
motivation: Reviewer anonymity may be weakened when authors and reviewers overlap in the same review cycle, since an anonymous review can potentially be associated with the reviewer's own submission and shrink the anonymity set.
method: The authors build the ECHO system, combining technical-expertise and writing-style signals across reviews, papers, and rebuttals, and evaluate it on R2S-Bench, a ground-truth benchmark constructed for this task.
result: ECHO identifies the reviewer's own submission in the Top-1 for 34.6% of reviews, Top-5 for 54.0%, and Top-10 for 63.4%, far above random ranking; a stronger Stage-2 reranker raises performance to 56.4% Top-1 and 66.4% Top-10.
conclusion: Review-to-submission linkage is practically feasible using only routinely released peer-review artifacts, revealing a deanonymization risk in anonymous peer review.

title: Natural Deduction Derivations As Directed Acyclic Proof Graphs
authors: Aaron Stump Jonathan Chan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In conventional natural deduction, a proof of a proposition is a derivation tree constructed out of inference rules with some number of premises and a conclusion judgement. For propositional logic, in contrast to the other connectives, the rule for disjunction elimination of [MATH] involves concluding with an auxiliary formula C from [MATH] and [MATH]. Not only is this asymmetry unsightly, it also introduces the need for commuting conversions across disjunction eliminations to transform between proof derivations that are morally equivalent but not [MATH]-equivalent. To resolve the asymmetry, Jean-Yves Girard suggests a disjunction elimination rule with multiple conclusions A and B, but claims that "we have no way of bringing them back together". In this work, we pursue Girard's proposal using the key insight that proof derivations need not be trees, but may be directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in general. Derivation rules are represented as nodes, premises as incoming edges, and conclusions as outgoing edges. Treating derivations as DAGs permits using the alternate rule by ensuring that the subderivations pointed at by each conclusion eventually join up at a new concluding node. Commuting conversions can then be formulated in terms of interactions with this join node. We explore ways to design a proof graph language with reduction and commutation rules such that proof simplification retains its concluding judgements, i.e. type preservation. In particular, we examine two styles of reduction rules: a local style, which only requires looking at the relevant subgraph of a whole proof but necessitates a number of extraneous constructs to satisfy type preservation; and a global style, which doesn't require all the extraneous constructs but necessitates looking at the entire proof graph as a whole.
tldr: The paper reformulates natural deduction derivations as directed acyclic proof graphs, following Girard's suggestion of a multi-conclusion disjunction elimination rule.
motivation: Conventional natural deduction treats disjunction elimination asymmetrically, requiring commuting conversions to relate morally equivalent but non-identical derivations; Girard proposed a multi-conclusion rule but claimed the conclusions could not be brought back together.
method: Derivations are represented as DAGs where rules are nodes, premises are incoming edges, and conclusions are outgoing edges; a join node reunites the multiple conclusions, and two styles of reduction rules (local and global) are designed to preserve type preservation.
result: The authors develop a proof graph language with reduction and commutation rules, showing that local-style reductions require extraneous constructs for type preservation while global-style reductions avoid them at the cost of inspecting the whole graph.
conclusion: Treating derivations as DAGs resolves the asymmetry of disjunction elimination and provides a framework for formulating commuting conversions via join nodes, with trade-offs between local and global reduction styles.

title: A Combined Streaming Fpga Architecture For Client-Side Ckks Encoding And Encryption
authors: Joseph Kurina, Bogdan Pasca, Suleyman Demirsoy, Sunwoong Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Homomorphic encryption allows a computing service to process encrypted data, but the client must first encode and encrypt its inputs. Sharing hardware between floating-point encoding and modular encryption reduces area but requires those transform roles to execute at different times. We present a streaming FPGA architecture for CKKS encoding and encryption that computes the shared floating-point encoding transform once and performs the integer transforms for six residue moduli in parallel. Dedicated transform pipelines exchange intermediate results on chip rather than through off-chip memory. DSP Builder generates the transform RTL, and Altera HLS IP Gen compiler compiles the surrounding SYCL pipeline into IP integrated with DMA and control logic in an accelerator functional unit. At polynomial degree N = 8192, the Altera Agilex 7 implementation delivers 5,143 complete ciphertexts per second at 471 MHz. One SEAL-Embedded CPU worker on the same workstation delivers 113 ciphertexts per second for real-valued inputs using all 4,096 slots. Measurements cover prepared-input computation through complete ciphertext construction, including FPGA submission and output delivery.
tldr: The paper presents a streaming FPGA architecture that accelerates client-side CKKS encoding and encryption for homomorphic encryption.
motivation: Homomorphic encryption requires clients to encode and encrypt inputs before outsourcing computation, and sharing hardware between floating-point encoding and modular encryption can reduce area if scheduled carefully.
method: The architecture computes the shared floating-point encoding transform once, performs integer transforms for six residue moduli in parallel using dedicated on-chip transform pipelines, and integrates DSP Builder RTL with a SYCL-based HLS pipeline plus DMA and control logic.
result: At polynomial degree N = 8192 on an Altera Agilex 7 FPGA at 471 MHz, the design delivers 5,143 complete ciphertexts per second, compared with 113 ciphertexts per second from one SEAL-Embedded CPU worker on the same workstation.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a high-throughput FPGA accelerator for CKKS client-side encoding and encryption, but it is a classical homomorphic-encryption hardware engineering contribution with no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: AutoRedClaw: Automated Red-Teaming For Claw-Style Agents
authors: Hao Li, Tongyan Hu, Weidi Luo, Shanghao Shi, Xiaogeng Liu, Aiden Suh, Yulong Cao, Ning Zhang, William Yeoh, Yevgeniy Vorobeychik, Chaowei Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent systems are shifting from task-scoped tool-use agents to persistent, personalized assistants such as OpenClaw. These claw-style agents maintain configuration files (e.g., AGENTS.md), long-term memory, and reusable skills. Once poisoned, this persistent state is repeatedly reloaded into the agent's context, creating persistent threats across tasks and sessions. Existing security evaluation systems struggle to evaluate these complex claw-style systems since they rely heavily on manually constructed test cases and environments, which limits their scale and coverage; in addition, these manually designed cases quickly become outdated as agents evolve, and their evaluation settings leave a gap with how claw-style agents are deployed in practice. To address this, we introduce AutoRedClaw, an automated red-teaming framework that generates end-to-end attacks together with the environments needed to execute them. AutoRedClaw combines a strict quality-checking protocol with execution-based validation to ensure the correctness, realism, and effectiveness of generated samples, and adopts task-driven environment construction to keep costs low. To achieve broad coverage, it organizes generation along risk categories, attack strategies, attack stages, and attack surfaces, and uses experience-guided exploration to steer generation toward under-explored regions. AutoRedClaw achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at less than $0.10 per successful sample. From its outputs, we construct RedClaw-Bench, a 330-case benchmark that yields substantially higher attack success rates (ASRs) than AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTap. Across seven harnesses and four frontier models, most agent systems exceed 50% ASR, showing that our red-teaming pipeline provides a strong evaluation signal even for the most advanced agent systems. Our code and benchmark are released at [URL].
tldr: AutoRedClaw is an automated red-teaming framework that generates end-to-end attacks, together with execution environments, against persistent 'claw-style' LLM agents, and it is used to build the 330-case RedClaw-Bench benchmark.
motivation: Persistent agent systems such as OpenClaw keep configuration files, long-term memory, and reusable skills that, once poisoned, are reloaded across sessions and thereby create durable threats, yet existing security evaluations rely on manual test cases that scale poorly and drift from real deployments.
method: The framework pairs a strict quality-checking protocol with execution-based validation, constructs environments in a task-driven way to keep costs low, and organizes generation along risk categories, attack strategies, attack stages, and attack surfaces, with experience-guided exploration pushing toward under-explored regions.
result: AutoRedClaw achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at under $0.10 per successful sample, and the derived RedClaw-Bench yields substantially higher ASRs than AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTap, with most of the seven harnesses and four frontier models exceeding 50% ASR.
conclusion: Automated, environment-generating red-teaming gives a strong and scalable evaluation signal for the security of persistent LLM agent systems.

title: Privacy-Preserving Robustness-Guided Testing
authors: Charles Koll, Houssam Abbas, Mike Rosulek
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In industries like semi-conductors and aerospace, it is common for the design company to contract out part of the testing process to a Testing-as-a-Service (TaaS) company. In such a setup, both parties want to keep their intellectual property private (i.e. unknown to the other party): namely the design and its output traces for the designer, and the detailed correctness specifications for the tester. We demonstrate a practical way for conducting provably private TaaS using a cryptographically secure multi-party computation protocol. We do so for the common setup where the specification is in Signal Temporal Logic, and testing is done using robustness-guided falsification. Our implementation carefully separates the steps of falsification, and manages to be [MATH], in the sense that the parties learn the absolutely minimum necessary for falsification. For up to a 100-dimensional input search space, the generation of one test takes less than 80 msec, and the overhead of the privacy-preserving protocol is less than 6x. These numbers mean that privacy-preserving TaaS is practical, thus enabling TaaS in security-sensitive industries.
tldr: The paper presents a privacy-preserving Testing-as-a-Service protocol in which a design company and a testing contractor use secure multi-party computation to run robustness-guided falsification of Signal Temporal Logic specifications without revealing their private design, traces, or specifications.
motivation: In security-sensitive industries such as semiconductors and aerospace, outsourcing testing exposes valuable intellectual property, namely the design and its output traces on the designer's side and the detailed correctness specifications on the tester's side, so a practical method is needed for both parties to collaborate without disclosure.
method: The authors decompose robustness-guided falsification into distinct steps and implement each as a cryptographically secure multi-party computation protocol, keeping the specification in Signal Temporal Logic and revealing only the minimum information required to complete falsification.
result: For input search spaces up to 100 dimensions, generating a single test takes under 80 ms, and the privacy overhead is below 6x compared with the non-private baseline.
conclusion: Privacy-preserving Testing-as-a-Service is practical and could enable outsourced testing in security-sensitive industries, though the contribution lies in classical secure computation and formal-methods testing rather than in quantum information science.

title: Sre: Accelerating Zero-Knowledge Proofs Via Scalar Redundancy Elimination In Multi-Scalar Multiplication
authors: Jonathan Ku, Guanglei Zhou, Jiawen Wu, Junyao Zhang, Haoxuan Shan, Changchun Zhou, JV Rajendran, Yiran Chen, Hai Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-Scalar Multiplication (MSM) is a fundamental cryptographic operation used in Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) across a wide range of applications. Its computation involves intensive elliptic curve point additions (PADD). MSM plays a critical role in cryptographic primitives such as polynomial commitments and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), where it often becomes the runtime bottleneck. Consequently, optimizing MSM is an active area of research focused on reducing computational complexity and accelerating performance. The current state-of-the-art algorithm for large-scale MSM is Pippenger's bucket method, which consists of three main steps: point merging, bucket aggregation, and window aggregation. Among these, the point merging step is the primary performance bottleneck. Our work targets this major computational bottleneck. To reduce operations for practical applications, we propose a novel Scalar Redundancy Elimination (SRE) algorithm with three approaches: a vanilla array-based approach, a list-based greedy approach, and a list-based exhaustive approach, all incorporating an early stopping technique. Depending on the use case, these strategies can be integrated into our modified MSM algorithm, which is based on Pippenger's bucket method. As a result, our proposed MSM algorithm, enhanced with the SRE technique, incurs less than [MATH] additional search time, while reducing the number of operations by [MATH], leading to a [MATH] speedup in runtime compared to the standard Pippenger's bucket method. This translates to a [MATH] runtime reduction in various ZKP systems that rely heavily on MSM.
tldr: The paper proposes Scalar Redundancy Elimination (SRE) techniques to accelerate multi-scalar multiplication (MSM) in zero-knowledge proof systems by reducing elliptic curve point additions in Pippenger's bucket method.
motivation: MSM is a runtime bottleneck in zero-knowledge proofs and elliptic curve cryptography, and the point-merging step of Pippenger's bucket method is the primary performance bottleneck.
method: The authors introduce three SRE variants—array-based vanilla, list-based greedy, and list-based exhaustive—with early stopping, and integrate them into a modified Pippenger bucket-method MSM algorithm.
result: The enhanced MSM algorithm incurs less than some additional search time while reducing operation count substantially, yielding runtime speedups over standard Pippenger and translating to runtime reductions in ZKP systems.
conclusion: Scalar redundancy elimination can practically accelerate MSM and thus improve the performance of zero-knowledge proof systems that rely heavily on MSM.

title: Dista-lp: Privacy-Preserving Distributed Linear Programming For Metric Differential Privacy
authors: Michael Oluwole, Ruiyao Liu, Aleksander Stevens, Chenxi Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear-programming (LP) mechanisms for metric differential privacy (mDP) enable fine-grained, task-aware utility control, but they are computationally expensive and become privacy-fragile in distributed settings: uploading user-specific LP coefficient matrices (e.g., distance and loss blocks) to a central solver can itself leak sensitive information. We present DISTA-LP, a privacy-preserving distributed mDP optimization framework that replaces raw coefficient uploads with compact surrogate parameterizations and releases only calibrated, perturbed parameter vectors, thereby reducing both upload-stage leakage and problem dimensionality. On the server side, DISTA-LP reconstructs approximate coefficients and solves a scalable mastersubproblem formulation via Benders decomposition. To certify end-to-end privacy, we introduce a probabilistic mDP (PmDP) auditor that empirically quantifies the privacy loss induced by parameter release, allocates the required privacy budget prior to optimization, and composes it with the downstream mechanism to obtain an end-to-end mDP guarantee.
