Experiments on large realworld road-network datasets (Rome, New York City, and London) show that DISTA-LP achieves near-zero mDP violation rates, substantially reduces computation time compared to monolithic and hybrid baselines, and matches or improves utility, thereby demonstrating stronger upload privacy and significantly improved scalability.
tldr: DISTA-LP is a distributed, privacy-preserving framework for solving linear-programming mechanisms under metric differential privacy, using surrogate parameter releases and Benders decomposition.
motivation: LP-based metric differential privacy gives fine-grained utility control but is computationally expensive, and uploading users' raw LP coefficient matrices to a central solver leaks sensitive information.
method: The framework replaces raw coefficient uploads with compact surrogate parameterizations and releases only calibrated, perturbed parameter vectors; the server reconstructs approximate coefficients and solves a scalable master-subproblem via Benders decomposition, with a probabilistic mDP (PmDP) auditor allocating and composing privacy budgets end-to-end.
result: Experiments on Rome, NYC, and London road networks show near-zero mDP violation rates, substantially reduced computation time versus monolithic and hybrid baselines, and matching or improved utility.
conclusion: DISTA-LP achieves stronger upload-stage privacy and significantly better scalability for distributed metric-DP linear programming, though the work lies entirely in classical privacy-preserving optimization.

title: Secure Multimodal Federated Optimization Via Hierarchical DNA-Based Key Management
authors: Yaochu Jin Yuping Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated optimization over heterogeneous multimodal data enables distributed institutions to collaboratively optimize a shared model using medical images, genomic profiles, clinical records, and physiological signals without centralizing raw data. However, protecting modality-specific data throughout the optimization lifecycle remains insufficiently explored, particularly when heterogeneous modalities require separate encryption keys and selective local access. This paper proposes a secure multimodal federated optimization framework that separates local data protection from federated-update protection. A trusted key-management authority securely provisions one client key through Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE), from which each client locally derives modality-specific symmetric keys using the domain-separated HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF). Heterogeneous modalities are mapped into a unified DNA-domain representation and processed through a DNA-origami-inspired structural transformation before authenticated encryption with AES-GCM. During local optimization, only the required modalities are decrypted within an authorized client environment. Individual model updates are independently protected through secure aggregation, allowing the coordinator to observe only aggregated updates rather than each client's contribution. Together, these components establish a structured approach to modality-specific protection and secure collaborative optimization, integrating hierarchical key management, authenticated local encryption, and aggregation-level update protection within a unified framework.
tldr: The paper proposes a classical secure multimodal federated optimization framework using hierarchical DNA-inspired key management, HPKE, HKDF, AES-GCM, and secure aggregation.
motivation: Federated optimization over heterogeneous multimodal medical data requires protecting modality-specific data and model updates without centralizing raw data, but existing approaches insufficiently address separate encryption keys and selective local access.
method: A trusted authority provisions one client key via HPKE; clients derive modality-specific symmetric keys using HKDF, map modalities into a DNA-domain representation with DNA-origami-inspired transformation, encrypt with AES-GCM, and protect updates through secure aggregation.
result: The framework integrates hierarchical key management, authenticated local encryption, and aggregation-level update protection, allowing only required modalities to be decrypted locally and only aggregated updates to be observed by the coordinator.
conclusion: The work provides a structured classical security approach for multimodal federated optimization, but it does not address quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Make The Adversary Spend More Energy: Generative Deception Against Language-Model Attackers In Critical Infrastructure
authors: Vlad Mihal, Hosam Alamleh, Alessandro Cantelli-Forti
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model attackers consume computational resources as they explore and interact with a target, creating an opportunity for cyber deception to impose costs. Whether such engagements favor the defender requires measuring both sides. We evaluate an autonomous language-model attacker against a decoy that uses a defending language model to analyze attacker commands and select defensive responses. Across 330 sessions, eight model pairs, two attacker profiles and three counter-injection levels, both sides run on identical GPUs and their energy is measured above idle. With runtime thinking disabled, the attacker-to-defender energy ratio has a 95% interval above one in 41 of 48 configurations under an allocation excluding attacker diagnostic calls, and in all 48 when those calls are included. Token ratios remain within approximately a factor of two in configurations without generation-cap truncation, showing that token counts can obscure substantial energy asymmetry. Counter-injection increases attacker tokens by approximately 9% per level without a detectable pooled change in energy consumption. Enabling thinking on both sides increases defender energy by 8--17 times and reverses the exchange for one model pair in the original campaign. We use these findings to motivate a proposed SCADA deception architecture with private physical state per identified adversary and deterministic protocol and process emulation.
tldr: The paper measures energy consumption asymmetry between language-model attackers and defending decoys in cyber deception for critical infrastructure.
motivation: Language-model attackers consume computational resources during exploration, so cyber deception may impose costs on attackers if defenders can make engagements energetically unfavorable.
method: The authors run 330 sessions across eight model pairs, two attacker profiles, and three counter-injection levels on identical GPUs, measuring attacker and defender energy above idle.
result: The attacker-to-defender energy ratio exceeds one in most configurations, token ratios can obscure energy asymmetry, and enabling thinking increases defender energy by 8–17 times while reversing the exchange for one model pair.
conclusion: The findings motivate a SCADA deception architecture with private physical state per adversary and deterministic protocol/process emulation.

title: Space Complexity Of Reachability In Simple Path Graphs
authors: Chandana Sasidharan Krishnamoorthy Dinesh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One of the central questions in space complexity is whether nondeterministic logspace computations ([MATH]) can be simulated in unambiguous logspace ([MATH]). A stronger notion, ([MATH]), requires every configuration reachable from the start to have exactly one computation path (Buntrock et.al. 91). While directed graph reachability is [MATH]-complete, planar graph reachability is in [MATH] and undirected graph reachability is in deterministic logspace ([MATH]). In this work, we study the space complexity of reachability problem for restricted directed graph families and show the following. - For reach unambiguous graphs (graphs with at most one path from start vertex to every vertex), Lange (Lange 97) showed that reachability is in [MATH]. As our main result, we show that for simple path graphs (introduced in Kannan et.al. 08), which contains reach unambiguous graphs), where each vertex has at most one simple path from the start, we show that the reachability problem lies in [MATH]. - Our first result can also be equivalently stated as: the recognition problem for simple path is in [MATH] if and only if the reachability problem restricted to simple path graphs is also in [MATH]. Inspired by this, we investigate the complexity of graph recognition versus graph reachability for graph classes. Observe that for any graph class, solving reachability (for the class) also solves the recognition problem for that class. We show that for reach unambiguous graphs, solving recognition is as hard as solving reachability (making both of them [MATH]-complete). (Abstract shortened to meet arXiv limits).
tldr: This paper studies the space complexity of the graph reachability problem restricted to simple path graphs, showing that reachability for such graphs lies in unambiguous logspace.
motivation: The central open question of whether nondeterministic logspace equals unambiguous logspace motivates studying reachability on restricted directed graph families where structural constraints may enable unambiguous simulation.
method: The authors analyze reachability and recognition problems for reach-unambiguous graphs and simple path graphs (each vertex has at most one simple path from the start), proving containment results and equivalences between recognition and reachability complexity.
result: Reachability on simple path graphs is shown to be in unambiguous logspace, and for reach-unambiguous graphs recognition is shown to be as hard as reachability (both complete for the class).
conclusion: The work clarifies the space complexity landscape for restricted graph reachability and connects graph recognition complexity with reachability complexity for structured graph classes.

title: Data-driven Accelerated Multigrid Method For Riesz Space Fractional Diffusion Equations
authors: Juan Zhang Yang Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The multigrid method is one of the most efficient iterative methods for solving large structured linear systems, and its efficiency stems from the complementarity between the smoother and the coarse grid correction. In this paper, we consider the block Toeplitz linear system obtained by discretizing time dependent Riesz space fractional diffusion equations, and employ the weighted Jacobi iterative method as a smoother. The weighted Jacobi smoother features a simple structure and low computational cost, yet its smoothing property is highly dependent on the relaxation parameter. We adopt Gaussian process regression to select the relaxation parameter to accelerate the convergence of the multigrid method. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical analysis, which simultaneously verifies the effectiveness and superiority of the data-driven parameter selection strategy.
tldr: A data-driven multigrid solver for Riesz space fractional diffusion equations that uses Gaussian process regression to tune the weighted Jacobi relaxation parameter.
motivation: Multigrid efficiency hinges on the interplay between smoother and coarse-grid correction, but the weighted Jacobi smoother's performance depends sensitively on its relaxation parameter, which is hard to choose optimally.
method: The block Toeplitz system arising from discretizing time-dependent Riesz space fractional diffusion equations is solved with multigrid, using weighted Jacobi as smoother and Gaussian process regression to select the relaxation parameter.
result: Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical analysis and show that the data-driven parameter selection speeds up multigrid convergence and outperforms baseline choices.
conclusion: Learning the smoothing parameter via Gaussian process regression yields an effective and superior multigrid solver for fractional diffusion problems.

title: Canard Points In Planar Mass-action Networks: A Flux Criterion, A Duality, And A Complete Classification
authors: Andrei-Dan Halanay Miruna-Mihaela Beldiman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine which mass-action reaction networks on two species, one fast and one slow, admit a canard point: a singular Hopf bifurcation at a fold of the critical manifold, followed by a canard explosion. In flux coordinates, existence reduces to three linear equations, one linear inequation and a sign condition on the product of two linear forms, and the criticality of the explosion is the sign of an explicit cubic form. For four reactions with a balance matrix of full rank, both become integer polynomial conditions on the stoichiometry. A vacancy duality, which exchanges the activator-inhibitor and substrate-depletion mechanisms, preserves canard points together with their criticality. The central structural result is a mode criterion: a network has a canard point if and only if its elementary flux modes contain a sign-meeting pair and a mode carrying a fold. Hence every canard network contains a minimal one carried by at most three modes, and so by at most twelve reactions, whatever the molecularity. For complexes of molecularity at most three we enumerate all 138,754 minimal canard networks and label each exactly by the criticalities it admits. None has more than six reactions; 32 have canard points of codimension zero and no explosion; and most six-reaction networks admit both criticalities, separated by degenerate canard points. All labels rest on exact certificates.
tldr: The paper classifies planar mass-action reaction networks that admit canard points and canard explosions using flux coordinates and elementary flux modes.
motivation: Canard points are important in singular perturbation dynamics, but a general structural characterization for mass-action networks was lacking.
method: The authors reduce canard existence to linear and sign conditions in flux coordinates and derive a mode criterion based on elementary flux modes, enabling exact enumeration for small complexes.
result: They show canard networks are characterized by sign-meeting pairs and fold-carrying flux modes, classify all 138,754 minimal canard networks for molecularity at most three, and give exact criticality labels.
conclusion: The work provides a complete algebraic and combinatorial classification of canard points in planar mass-action networks, with a duality relating activator-inhibitor and substrate-depletion mechanisms.

title: Beta-expansions Induced By General Parry Polynomials And Sharp Iteration Asymptotics Of Their Transfer Operators
authors: Horia D. Cornean, Ira W. Herbst, Kasper S. S{\o}rensen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper generalizes previous results to any Parry polynomials [MATH] of finite degree [MATH]. Let [MATH] be the unique positive root of [MATH] and consider the transfer operator [MATH] induced by the map [MATH]. Suppose all other roots of [MATH] have magnitude less than one. Then for any smooth function [MATH] on [MATH] we prove two term asymptotics in [MATH] of the form \big(^r(F)\big)(\cdot)= u(\cdot) \int_0^1 F(x)\: x +\beta^{-r}v(\cdot) \big (F(1)-F(0)\big )+o(\beta^{-r}),\quad r\geq 1, where [MATH] is piecewise constant and [MATH], while [MATH] is piecewise equal to a polynomial of degree one and [MATH]. When [MATH] is restricted to functions of bounded variation [MATH], it is known that [MATH] contains its essential spectrum. Thus the contribution coming from [MATH] in the above estimate is not guaranteed if [MATH] is not smooth enough. Furthermore, we show that when [MATH] is restricted to [MATH] then any [MATH] is an eigenvalue with infinite multiplicity. Moreover, we construct a meromorphic extension of [MATH] to the domain [MATH], where the finite rank poles are numbers [MATH] with [MATH] such that [MATH] is a root of [MATH]. If such poles [MATH] other than [MATH] exist, then we construct eigenvectors of [MATH] in [MATH] obeying [MATH], where [MATH] is given by series involving the values of [MATH] taken in some specially chosen, finer and finer partitions of [MATH]. When [MATH] is either a polynomial or a characteristic function like [MATH], then [MATH] can be explicitly computed.
tldr: The paper proves sharp two-term asymptotics for transfer operators associated with beta-expansions induced by general Parry polynomials and analyzes their spectral and meromorphic properties.
motivation: The work extends prior results on beta-expansions and transfer operators from restricted settings to arbitrary Parry polynomials of finite degree, aiming to characterize asymptotic behavior and spectral structure.
method: It studies the transfer operator induced by the beta-transformation, proving asymptotics for smooth functions and bounded variation functions, constructing meromorphic extensions, and analyzing eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
result: For smooth functions, the transfer operator has a two-term asymptotic expansion involving a piecewise constant function and a piecewise linear function; for bounded variation functions, essential spectrum appears, and additional eigenvalues with infinite multiplicity are shown under certain restrictions.
conclusion: The paper provides a detailed spectral and asymptotic analysis of transfer operators for general Parry polynomials, with explicit computations in special cases such as polynomials or characteristic functions.

title: Front-pinned Spectral Collocation For The Flame Problem And Related Ignition Problems
authors: Imre Boros
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider global Chebyshev collocation for the ignition problems [MATH], [MATH], [MATH]; for [MATH] this is the flame problem, a standard stiff test equation. After rescaling to [MATH] the solution has an interior layer of width [MATH], [MATH], at a [MATH]-dependent position. Two obstacles arise: plain Chebyshev collocation needs [MATH] nodes, and imposing the initial condition amplifies errors by a factor of order [MATH], which makes the collocation equations severely ill-conditioned. Our main contribution addresses the second one. Since all solutions are translates of one profile, the initial condition can be replaced by an equivalent interior condition. For an unknown [MATH], imposing it where the speed [MATH] of [MATH] along the orbit is maximal bounds the propagator of the linearized equation by one; for [MATH] this is [MATH]. For the first obstacle we use the sinh map of Tee and Trefethen: the time function is explicit, the complex singularities of the profile lie exactly at [MATH], and the map parameters follow in closed form, so that [MATH] nodes suffice. In double precision the pinned scheme reaches the interpolation error of the exact solution in five or six Newton iterations for [MATH] down to [MATH], whereas the initial-condition form fails or converges to wrong discrete solutions, also in an integral (Birkhoff) reformulation. Computations in [MATH]-bit arithmetic confirm the predicted rate down to errors of [MATH], AAA approximation locates the singularities to within [MATH], and the method carries over to an Arrhenius reaction rate, with all parameters computed numerically.
tldr: A numerical analysis paper developing a front-pinned Chebyshev spectral collocation method for stiff flame and ignition problems.
motivation: The flame problem is a standard stiff test equation whose solution has a narrow interior layer, and standard Chebyshev collocation suffers from ill-conditioning when imposing the initial condition.
method: The authors replace the initial condition with an equivalent interior condition pinned where the solution speed along the orbit is maximal, and use a sinh map of Tee and Trefethen to resolve the interior layer with few nodes.
result: The pinned scheme reaches interpolation error in five or six Newton iterations for small epsilon down to 1e-10, while the initial-condition form fails or converges to wrong discrete solutions; high-precision computations confirm the predicted convergence rate.
conclusion: Front-pinned spectral collocation is an effective numerical method for the flame problem and related ignition problems, and it extends to Arrhenius reaction rates.

title: Higher Tripos Theory
authors: Yoshihiro Maruyama
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tripos theory constructs categorical models of higher-order logic from indexed logical data. We develop higher tripos theory and higher tripos-to-topos construction recovering the classical construction on zero-types through a covering criterion. The higher tripos-to-topos construction yields elementary [MATH]-toposes with closed bounded hierarchies of univalent universes, thus establishing a logical adjunction between [MATH]-triposes and elementary [MATH]-toposes with univalent universes. We also construct a logically conservative higher completion of regular [MATH]-categories with weak section families and a finite-limit-closed projective cover. This completion preserves original maps, predicates, and existing dependent products, and gives criteria for extending interpretations while preserving logical structure. With strongly inaccessible size bounds, Kleene assemblies instantiate the construction, producing a cumulative hierarchy of univalent universes that classifies every family in the completion and recovering the effective topos as the category of zero-types. We then establish an arithmetical completeness result: for a uniformly computably presented family, the numerical index set for identity with a fixed classifier code is [MATH]-complete. We also construct two inequivalent univalent classifiers with the same global homotopy type: every internal map from one to the natural-number object is constant, whereas the other admits a nonconstant such map. These reconstruction, preservation, and computability results contribute to the higher effective-topos program of Awodey-Emmenegger and Anel-Awodey-Barton.
tldr: The paper develops higher tripos theory and a higher tripos-to-topos construction, yielding elementary infinity-toposes with hierarchies of univalent universes, plus a conservative completion of regular infinity-categories and arithmetic completeness results for Kleene assemblies.
motivation: Tripos theory provides categorical models of higher-order logic from indexed logical data; the authors aim to lift the classical zero-type tripos-to-topos construction to a higher-categorical setting, extending the higher effective-topos program of Awodey-Emmenegger and Anel-Awodey-Barton.
method: The authors introduce higher triposes, define a tripos-to-topos construction controlled by a covering criterion, and build a logically conservative completion of regular infinity-categories with weak section families and finite-limit-closed projective covers; Kleene assemblies with strongly inaccessible size bounds instantiate the construction.
result: The construction produces elementary infinity-toposes with closed bounded hierarchies of univalent universes and establishes a logical adjunction between infinity-triposes and such toposes; the numerical index set for identity with a fixed classifier code is shown to be complete for a uniformly computably presented family, and two inequivalent univalent classifiers with the same global homotopy type are constructed.
conclusion: The work supplies reconstruction, preservation, and computability results supporting the higher effective-topos program, recovering the effective topos as the category of zero-types.

title: Theorem Prover Arend
authors: Fedor Part, Valery Isaev, Sergey Sinchuk
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper is an exposition of the theorem prover Arend developed at JetBrains Research. Arend language has been designed to facilitate the formalization of mathematics within the framework of univalent foundations and with the focus on constructive mathematics. It is based on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax that is more closely aligned with Martin-L\"of Type Theory (MLTT) than fully computational cubical type theories, while still retaining some of their computational properties useful in practice. Among the most notable features of the Arend language is its powerful system of classes and records supporting subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations and anonymous extensions, which provides extensive flexibility for constructing hierarchies of definitions. Formalization in Arend is streamlined by the IntelliJ Arend plugin, which transforms IntelliJ IDEA into a full-fledged integrated development environment (IDE) for the Arend language. The main Arend library arend-lib includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology and synthetic homotopy theory.
tldr: This paper presents the Arend theorem prover, a dependently typed proof assistant based on homotopy type theory and cubical syntax for formalizing constructive mathematics.
motivation: The authors aim to expose the design and features of Arend, developed at JetBrains Research, to support formalization of mathematics within univalent foundations and constructive mathematics.
method: Arend is built on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax closer to Martin-Löf type theory, and provides a class/record system, subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations, anonymous extensions, and an IntelliJ-based IDE.
result: The paper describes Arend's language design, its practical computational properties, its IDE support via the IntelliJ Arend plugin, and its main library arend-lib containing formalizations in constructive algebra, topology, and synthetic homotopy theory.
conclusion: Arend is a practical proof assistant for univalent and constructive mathematics, but it is not related to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Matrix-Free Resolvent Analysis For Large-Scale Aerodynamic Systems
authors: Sicheng He Rohit Sunil Kanchi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: At industrial scale the cost of resolvent analysis is set by the linear solves and the assembly and storage of the Jacobian. We present a matrix-free resolvent framework in the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes solver ADflow: automatic differentiation supplies the action of the shifted Jacobian and its Hermitian transpose, preconditioned Krylov solves recycle subspaces across a Lanczos bidiagonalization, and every gain is certified by a backward error. It is applied to the NASA Common Research Model wing at Mach 0.85 and 4.2 degrees on three grid levels of 0.45, 3.6 and 28.8 million cells, the finest with 1.73x10^8 complex unknowns, 2.3 times the largest reported resolvent computation. On the coarsest level an unstable buffet mode makes the gain peak a resonance; on the finer two the operator is stable and the peak, 1.33x10^4 at omega = 6.4 and 3.0x10^3 near omega = 7.7, is a pseudo-resonance of damped modes whose buffet cells travel outboard at about 0.3 times the free-stream speed. Refinement turns an oscillator into an amplifier of the same mechanism, as forced simulations confirm. A certified frequency costs 3.6 minutes on 128 cores at 2.7 million unknowns, with 14 to 34 kB per unknown, nearly four orders of magnitude below a sparse factorization.
tldr: The authors present a matrix-free resolvent analysis framework in the RANS solver ADflow, scaling to 1.73x10^8 complex unknowns on the NASA Common Research Model wing.
motivation: At industrial scale, resolvent analysis is limited by the cost of linear solves and the assembly/storage of the Jacobian, motivating a matrix-free approach that avoids sparse factorization.
method: Automatic differentiation provides the action of the shifted Jacobian and its Hermitian transpose, preconditioned Krylov solves recycle subspaces across Lanczos bidiagonalization, and each gain is certified via backward error.
result: Computations on grids of 0.45, 3.6 and 28.8 million cells reveal a resonant unstable buffet mode on the coarsest grid and pseudo-resonant damped modes on finer grids, with certified frequencies costing 3.6 minutes on 128 cores and memory four orders of magnitude below sparse factorization.
conclusion: Grid refinement transforms an oscillator into an amplifier of the same buffet mechanism, confirming forced simulations and demonstrating the feasibility of large-scale matrix-free resolvent analysis.

title: When Weak Submodularity Meets Matroids: How Does Standard Greedy Behave?
authors: Qixin Zhang, Shi Fu, Shengminjie Chen, Chao Qian, Dacheng Tao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weakly submodular maximization finds numerous applications in machine learning, data mining and statistics. In particular, under a cardinality constraint, the standard greedy algorithm is known to attain the tight [MATH]-approximation guarantee, where [MATH] denotes the submodularity ratio. However, when considering general matroid constraints, has remained a longstanding open question. In this paper, we resolve this question by studying the worst-case approximation guarantee [MATH] of standard forward greedy, where [MATH] is the rank of matroid. Specifically, our first contribution is the following refined lower bound R_{\gr}(\gamma,r)\ge \max\left\{ {r}, {B_\gamma+}, } {2-\gamma+\gamma^{r+1}}, {14\left(B_\gamma+\right)} \right\}, where [MATH]. This lower bound not only strictly improves upon the previous guarantee of [MATH], but also can recover the classical [MATH]-approximation guarantee at [MATH]. Subsequently, a corresponding upper bound is established for [MATH], namely, R_{\gr}(\gamma,r) \le\min\left\{{2},20\max\left\{{r}, {B_\gamma+ }\right\}\right\}. For every fixed [MATH], this Eq. effectively sharpens the recent [MATH] upper bound to [MATH], where [MATH] is the size of ground set. Putting all these results together, we eventually can obtain \[R_{\gr}(\gamma,r) = \Theta\!\left( \max\left\{{r}, {1+}\right\} \right).\].
tldr: The paper resolves the open question of the worst-case approximation guarantee of the standard forward greedy algorithm for weakly submodular maximization under general matroid constraints, giving matching lower and upper bounds.
motivation: Weakly submodular maximization has many applications in machine learning, data mining, and statistics, but the greedy algorithm's approximation guarantee was only settled for cardinality constraints, leaving matroid constraints an open problem.
method: The authors derive a refined lower bound on the worst-case approximation ratio R_gr(gamma, r) of standard forward greedy as a function of the submodularity ratio gamma and matroid rank r, and complement it with a matching upper bound construction.
result: They obtain R_gr(gamma, r) = Theta(max{r, 1 + ...}), strictly improving prior guarantees, recovering the classical (1 - e^{-1}) guarantee in the appropriate limit, and sharpening the recent upper bound for every fixed gamma.
conclusion: The greedy algorithm's performance for weakly submodular maximization under matroid constraints is now characterized up to constants, closing a longstanding theoretical gap in submodular optimization.

title: Low Residuals, Wrong Value: Learning The Viscosity Solution Of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs Equations With PINNs
authors: Raul Jimenez, Pablo Tejerina-P\'erez, Leonid Sarieddine, Pedro Taranc\'on-\'alvarez, Marisol Traforetti, Pau Sol\'e-Vilar\'o, Oleksii Ignatenko, Nazar Tkach, Pavlos Protopapas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and other residual-trained solvers judge a candidate solution by the size of its sampled PDE residual. For first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations this is not sufficient: the same equation and boundary data admit Lipschitz almost-everywhere solutions that differ from the viscosity solution by [MATH] while violating the equation only on sets of measure zero. We study whether residual minimization selects such solutions in a fixed-horizon pursuit-evasion game whose Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs value function is known in closed form on the circle [MATH] and on the flat tori [MATH] and [MATH]. We train four neural parameterizations with ten seeds on each geometry, 120 runs in total. A standard network with periodic Fourier features converges to folded almost-everywhere solutions in all 30 runs: small residuals and the expected capture-layer gradient, yet values that are wrong over most of the domain. A network with periodicity imposed through the loss recovers the viscosity solution in one and two dimensions but becomes unreliable in four. Two parameterizations that receive the geodesic distance do substantially better: a single network fed the wrapped displacement and its distance recovers the viscosity solution in all 30 runs, while a minimum over periodic image charts succeeds in 27 of 30 and introduces a wrong-image failure mode. Finally, for the convex Hamiltonian considered here, we use the semiconcavity of the viscosity solution to build a mesh-free finite-difference test that needs only forward network evaluations; it detects the folded solutions and the harmful min-of-charts failures without access to the exact value function. A small sampled residual thus does not by itself validate a learned Hamilton-Jacobi solution; the parameterization and independent structural diagnostics can be essential for selecting the viscosity solution.
tldr: Residual-trained PINN solvers can converge to spurious Lipschitz almost-everywhere solutions of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations rather than the true viscosity solution, and parameterization choices plus structural diagnostics are needed to fix this.
motivation: Small sampled PDE residuals are commonly treated as validation for learned PDE solutions, but for first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations this criterion is insufficient because non-viscosity solutions can violate the equation only on measure-zero sets.
method: The authors train four neural parameterizations with ten seeds across three geometries (circle, two flat tori) for a pursuit-evasion game with a closed-form value function, totaling 120 runs, and additionally construct a mesh-free finite-difference test based on semiconcavity of the viscosity solution.
result: Standard Fourier-feature networks converge to folded almost-everywhere solutions in all 30 runs despite small residuals, while geodesic-distance-informed parameterizations recover the viscosity solution in 30/30 and 27/30 runs; the semiconcavity-based diagnostic detects the failures without access to the exact solution.
conclusion: A small sampled residual does not validate a learned Hamilton-Jacobi solution; parameterization design and independent structural diagnostics are essential for selecting the viscosity solution.

title: Graphexon Mean Field Games On Large Network Limits
authors: Minyi Huang Peter E. Caines
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper analyzes graphexon mean field games (GXMFG) on large network limits. By considering edge distributions of a sequence of finite graphs, we define the empirical graphexon measures and study their subsequential weak limits in a graphexon space consisting of all symmetric probability measures on [MATH]. This concept of network limits extends graphon theory to general, not necessarily dense, networks. To formulate the game using the graphexon limit, we exploit a useful property that a probability measure on a product space is the product of a probability kernel and a marginal distribution. Based on such graph limits and the probability kernel of the associated graphexon measure, we derive the GXMFG equations, and present a detailed analysis for the linear-quadratic case. For linear-quadratic models with finite populations residing over large networks, we use the GXMFG equations to construct decentralized strategies, for which an [MATH]-Nash equilibrium property is established.
tldr: The paper develops mean field game theory (GXMFG) on limits of large, possibly sparse networks characterized by 'graphexon' measures, extending graphon-based limits to general networks.
motivation: Classical graphon mean field games rely on dense graph limits, which fail to capture sparse or general network structures common in real large-scale systems; a broader limit object is needed.
method: The authors define empirical graphexon measures from edge distributions of finite graph sequences, take subsequential weak limits in a graphexon space, and use a product-measure/probability-kernel decomposition to derive the GXMFG equations, with a detailed linear-quadratic treatment.
result: For linear-quadratic models on large finite networks, decentralized strategies constructed from the GXMFG equations are shown to form an ε-Nash equilibrium.
conclusion: Graphexon limits provide a tractable and general framework for mean field games on non-dense networks, with verifiable equilibrium guarantees in the LQ setting.

title: Plasticity Of The Unit Sphere Of The Space $c_0$
authors: Olesia Zavarzina
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we prove that the unit sphere of the space [MATH] is plastic, i.e., every non-expansive bijection from this sphere onto itself is an isometry.
tldr: The paper proves that the unit sphere of the Banach space c0 is 'plastic', meaning every non-expansive bijection of the sphere onto itself is automatically an isometry.
motivation: Plasticity of the unit sphere is a rigidity property studied in the geometry of Banach spaces, motivated by the question of how much metric structure constrains self-mappings of classical sequence spaces.
method: A purely mathematical (functional-analytic) proof establishing that non-expansive bijections of the unit sphere of c0 must preserve distances, i.e., be isometries.
result: The unit sphere of c0 is shown to be plastic, extending the known class of Banach spaces whose spheres exhibit this rigidity.
conclusion: The result contributes to the nonlinear geometry of Banach spaces, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: How Intervention History Changes Ai Agent Sabotage On Subsequent Tasks
authors: Amirali Aghazadeh Daniel Saeedi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI control evaluations often reset agents' memory between tasks, although deployed agents may retain records of prior interventions. We ask whether learning that an earlier attack was caught changes an agent's ability to evade defer-to-trusted (DtT), a protocol that replaces suspicious work with a trusted model's solution. Herein, we study cross-episode adaptation: whether intervention history changes attack behavior on a subsequent task with different objectives and a fresh environment. We evaluate this using ControlArena's Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and SHADE-Arena as testbeds, where agents must complete a main task while covertly pursuing a harmful side objective. For each successor task, we pair a history-conditioned attempt with the model's no-history attempt. The retained history either states that the previous submission was replaced or additionally includes the trusted model's replacement. For Claude Opus 4.8 on IaC, intervention history reduces successful sabotage. Completion of both the main and side objectives falls from 77% to 12% when the agent is told about the replacement and to 38% when it is also shown the trusted model's replacement, while main task success remains essentially unchanged. Condensing the history weakens this effect, suggesting that the retained context matters and limiting attribution to intervention feedback alone. GPT-5.4 shows no significant change in successful sabotage on the same IaC benchmark. On SHADE-Arena, GPT-5's successful sabotage rate decreases, but the reduction is not significant. Across the tested models, history conditions, and deferral thresholds, intervention history never increases the rate of successful sabotage that survives DtT. These results show that intervention history can change subsequent attack behavior, but its effect depends on both the model and the retained context.
tldr: The paper studies whether an AI agent's retained intervention history (e.g., knowledge that a prior sabotage attempt was caught and replaced) changes its ability to evade a defer-to-trusted (DtT) control protocol on later tasks.
motivation: AI control evaluations typically reset agent memory between episodes, but deployed agents may carry records of past interventions; it is unknown whether such cross-episode adaptation alters attack behavior on subsequent, differently-scoped tasks.
method: Using ControlArena's Infrastructure-as-Code and SHADE-Arena testbeds, the authors pair history-conditioned attack attempts with no-history baselines across several models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.4, GPT-5), varying retained context (mention of replacement vs. full trusted-model replacement) and deferral thresholds.
result: For Claude Opus 4.8 on IaC, joint main+side objective completion drops from 77% to 12% (replacement notice) or 38% (with replacement shown) while main-task success is unchanged; GPT-5.4 shows no significant change, and SHADE-Arena results for GPT-5 are non-significant; history never increased successful sabotage.
conclusion: Intervention history can reduce subsequent successful sabotage, but the effect is model- and context-dependent, underscoring the need for careful design of retained context in AI control evaluations.

title: Profile-DP: Differential Privacy For User-Controlled Profile Release In Personalized Llm Inference
authors: Mingchen Li, Zifan Peng, Kewei Sha, Lavinia F Pieptea, Heng Fan, Junhua Ding, Meikang Qiu, Yunhe Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on profile-conditioned inference, pairing public requests with rich, user-specific facts. This paradigm exposes the user profile itself, together with the user's explicit sharing preferences. We introduce Profile-DP, a policy-aware local differential privacy framework designed specifically for user-profile release in personalized LLM inference. Profile-DP provably bounds the release of user-withheld facts while treating public instructions, profile schemas, and authorized facts as public side information. By generating a privatized profile that composes with the public instruction prior to answer generation, our framework decouples formal privacy guarantees from downstream model behavior. We develop two finite-domain mechanisms satisfying Profile-DP: DP-SLOT independently perturbs protected attributes, while DP-BLOCK uses public semantic decisions to coordinate their release and jointly sample related attributes. A positive, public compatibility prior connects these attributes while preserving a profile-level privacy bound. On PEEP, DP-BLOCK leads the utility composite among DP methods at all 13 structured budgets and is closest to the ideal privacy--utility point in 18 of 26 format--budget settings under our composite weighting. Direct measurements reveal complementary strengths: DP-BLOCK discloses less, while DP-SLOT retains more authorized facts. These results make policy-aware profile release a practical basis for studying privacy and personalization.
tldr: Profile-DP is a policy-aware local differential privacy framework for releasing user profiles in personalized LLM inference, with two finite-domain mechanisms (DP-SLOT and DP-BLOCK) that bound disclosure of user-withheld facts while preserving utility.
motivation: Personalized LLM inference conditions responses on rich user-specific profiles, which risks exposing the profile itself and the user's explicit sharing preferences; existing DP approaches do not handle policy-aware, attribute-structured profile release.
method: The authors formalize profile release as a local DP problem with public side information (instructions, schemas, authorized facts) and design DP-SLOT (independent per-attribute perturbation) and DP-BLOCK (semantic-coordinated joint sampling with a public compatibility prior), composing the privatized profile with the public instruction before generation.
result: On the PEEP benchmark, DP-BLOCK leads the utility composite among DP methods across all 13 structured budgets and is closest to the ideal privacy-utility point in 18 of 26 format-budget settings; DP-BLOCK discloses less while DP-SLOT retains more authorized facts.
conclusion: Policy-aware profile release is presented as a practical and formally grounded basis for studying the privacy-personalization trade-off in personalized LLM systems.

title: Exposing Vulnerability Monoculture Through Systemic Adversarial Robustness
authors: Leo Elmecker-Plakolm, Lukasz Szpruch, Avishek Joey Bose, Matthew Wicker
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beneath the apparent diversity of foundation models lies an increasingly homogeneous technical stack of common training pipelines, distillation methods, and data. These shared algorithmic choices can expose an otherwise distinct model ecosystem to concentrated risks leading to a vulnerability monoculture. Yet current practice in assessing adversarial robustness is restricted to individual robustness scores and attack transfer rates, leaving open the unexplored fundamental question: how many attacks suffice for catastrophic widespread compromise? In this paper, we investigate the empirical nature of shared vulnerabilities within a model pool and introduce Systemic Adversarial Robustness (SAR), a novel measure of shared vulnerability of a model pool through the attack diversity needed to exploit it. Specifically, SAR interpolates between single-attack transferability and independent per-model robustness: small values reveal a vulnerability monoculture, whereas large values indicate that failures are dispersed across models. We theoretically formulate SAR as a partial set-cover problem with provable approximation guarantees---enabling the development of scalable algorithms to empirically measure the systemic adversarial robustness. We empirically test the shared vulnerability of vision and large language models and characterize their shared collective vulnerability curve. Specifically, we demonstrate that model pools distilled from DeepSeek-R1 and Claude Opus 4.6 exhibit lower estimated systemic robustness than their corresponding parent pools, revealing a potential systemic cost of frontier-model distillation. Our framework seeks to establish vulnerability monoculture as a measurable target for a more wholistic adversarial evaluation of model populations.
tldr: The paper introduces Systemic Adversarial Robustness (SAR) to measure shared vulnerabilities across pools of foundation models and identifies vulnerability monocultures.
motivation: Foundation models share training pipelines, distillation methods, and data, which may create correlated adversarial weaknesses that individual robustness scores fail to capture.
method: The authors formalize SAR as a partial set-cover problem with approximation guarantees and develop scalable algorithms to estimate the attack diversity needed to compromise a model pool.
result: Experiments on vision and language model pools show that distilled model pools can have lower systemic robustness than their parent pools, revealing a potential systemic cost of frontier-model distillation.
conclusion: Vulnerability monoculture should be treated as a measurable target for holistic adversarial evaluation of model populations.

title: Fundamental Impossibility Results In Ai Safety: Trading Off Between Desiderata
authors: Ida Mattsson, Ratip Emin Berker, Emanuel Tewolde, Ioannis Anagnostides, Kiriaki Fragkia, Xinyu Liu, Alexander Heckett, Jiayuan Liu, Eden Hartman, Vojt\v{e}ch Kova\v{r}\'{i}k, Sven Neth, Maria-Florina Balcan, Tuomas Sandholm, Vincent Conitzer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Is there a fundamental tradeoff between desiderata for safe AI systems, such as harmlessness and helpfulness? We answer by formalizing the interaction between AI systems and users as a game with three players: a defender and an attacker that are computationally or informationally bounded, and an AI that provides public advice and is less constrained. Our main result shows that there is a fundamental tradeoff in providing advice that helps the defender while advice remains public. We also consider whether the information that the AI shares can be manipulated to benefit only the defender and conclude with a discussion of how we can use these results in designing safer AI systems.
tldr: The paper formalizes AI-user interaction as a three-player game between a bounded defender, a bounded attacker, and a less-constrained advice-giving AI, and proves a fundamental tradeoff between helpfulness and harmlessness when advice is public.
motivation: Practitioners hope for AI systems that are simultaneously helpful and harmless, but it is unclear whether such desiderata can be jointly achieved; the authors seek a formal, complexity-theoretic answer.
method: They model the interaction as a game with a computationally or informationally bounded defender and attacker plus a public-advice-providing AI, and analyze the achievable guarantees under these bounds.
result: They establish a fundamental impossibility/tradeoff: advice that benefits the defender cannot remain public without also benefiting the attacker, and they examine whether shared information can be manipulated to favor only the defender.
conclusion: The results give formal guidance for designing safer AI systems, indicating structural limits on what public AI advice can achieve.

title: Dynamic Regret And Tightened Constraint Violation For Communication-Efficient Distributed Online Bilevel Optimization
authors: Fan Li, Xinlei Yi, Guanghui Wen, Yang Shi, Tao Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the distributed online bilevel optimization problem with time-varying inequality constraints. In this setting, a multi-agent network is confronted with a hierarchical decision-making task characterized by coupling between the inner and outer optimization levels. We first propose a communication-efficient single-loop distributed online primal--dual algorithm based on communication compression, which tracks both the inner-level solution and the Hessian-inverse-vector product using only one update per-round. We show that this algorithm achieves a dynamic network regret bound of [MATH], where~[MATH], [MATH] is the outer-level path variation, [MATH] is the inner-level path variation, and [MATH] is the gradient path variation alongside a network cumulative constraint violation bound of [MATH], which is further reduced to [MATH] under Slater's condition. Furthermore, to eliminate the dependence of regret on the inner-level and gradient path variation, we propose a novel adaptive multi-loop distributed online algorithm to control the inner-level approximation accuracy at each round. By dynamically adjusting the number of inner-level updates based on a gradient-norm tolerance condition, this algorithm yields an improved dynamic network regret bound of [MATH] which depends solely on the outer-level path variation while maintaining the same network cumulative constraint violation bound. Finally, numerical simulations verify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.
tldr: This paper develops communication-efficient distributed online primal-dual algorithms for bilevel optimization with time-varying inequality constraints, achieving dynamic network regret and tightened cumulative constraint violation bounds.
motivation: Distributed online bilevel optimization captures hierarchical multi-agent decision-making with coupled inner and outer problems, but existing methods suffer from high communication cost and regret that scales with inner-level and gradient path variation.
method: The authors propose a single-loop distributed online primal-dual algorithm using communication compression that tracks the inner-level solution and Hessian-inverse-vector product with one update per round, plus an adaptive multi-loop variant that dynamically sets inner-level update counts via a gradient-norm tolerance condition.
result: The single-loop method attains a dynamic network regret bound depending on outer-level, inner-level, and gradient path variation, with a cumulative constraint violation bound that tightens under Slater's condition; the multi-loop variant removes the dependence on inner-level and gradient path variation while preserving the violation bound.
conclusion: The proposed algorithms provide improved dynamic regret guarantees with reduced communication overhead for distributed online bilevel constrained optimization, verified numerically, but the work is purely classical optimization with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Multi-time-stepping Splitting Scheme With Mass Lumping For The Multiscale Wave Equation
authors: Yating Wang, Wing Tat Leung, Zhengya Yang, Shufan Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient simulation of wave propagation in high-contrast media is challenging because standard explicit schemes are subject to severe time-step restrictions induced by fine spatial scales and fast multiscale modes, whereas fully implicit schemes require costly globally coupled solves. In this work, we develop a mass-lumped multi-time-stepping partially explicit splitting method for multiscale wave equations. Based on a nonlocal multicontinuum (NLMC) decomposition of the approximation space, the solution is separated into contrast-dependent fast components and contrast-independent slow components, which are advanced implicitly and explicitly, respectively. A mass-lumping approximation diagonalizes the coarse-scale mass operator and removes the coupling between two subproblems, thus enabling multirate time integration for the two parts. To further improve efficiency, we introduce a residual-based adaptive strategy that dynamically adjusts the time step of the explicitly treated subsystem according to its temporal error indicator. The proposed scheme is shown to be energy stable under suitable assumptions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed mass-lumped multi-time-stepping scheme substantially reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of standard fully implicit methods.
tldr: The paper develops a mass-lumped multi-time-stepping partially explicit splitting scheme for efficiently simulating multiscale wave propagation in high-contrast media.
motivation: Standard explicit schemes for high-contrast multiscale wave equations suffer from severe time-step restrictions, while fully implicit schemes require costly globally coupled solves.
method: Using a nonlocal multicontinuum decomposition, the solution is split into fast contrast-dependent and slow contrast-independent components, advanced implicitly and explicitly, respectively; mass lumping diagonalizes the coarse-scale mass operator and a residual-based adaptive time-stepping strategy improves efficiency.
result: The scheme is shown to be energy stable under suitable assumptions, and numerical experiments demonstrate substantial computational cost reduction while maintaining accuracy comparable to fully implicit methods.
conclusion: The proposed mass-lumped multirate splitting method provides an efficient and stable numerical approach for multiscale wave equations in high-contrast media.

title: Evidence-Grounded LLM-Assisted Android Mobile Forensic Reporting
authors: Madhab Chandra Das, Sajid Ahmed, Tasnia Tabassum, Qingzhong Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can assist forensic report drafting, but fluent output does not ensure evidentiary reliability. This study presents an evidence-grounded framework for evaluating LLM-assisted Android forensic reports at the atomic-claim level. Gemini, Llama, and Qwen each generated reports for two controlled cases: a public Android 13 dataset and a physical LG device with a zero-reportable-fact boundary. The six accepted reports were decomposed into 612 claims and evaluated against frozen, human-reviewed authorities through content labeling, citation validation, fact-recall analysis, independent rechecking, and dispute resolution. The final corpus contained 424 supported, 163 unsupported, four contradicted, four overstated or incomplete, and 17 excluded claims. In the public case, all three models recovered all 27 authorized report-level facts. Citation validity nevertheless differed substantially: Gemini produced 168 valid citations from 189 required citations, Qwen produced 145 from 189, and Llama produced none from 135. In the physical device case, the models generated 65 claims despite the zero reportable-fact boundary, including 38 unsupported and one contradicted claim. These results show that evidence restriction and complete fact recall do not guarantee claim support or valid evidence attribution. The framework provides an auditable method for detecting unsupported content, preserving claim-to evidence lineage, and retaining investigator authority over final forensic reports.
tldr: The paper proposes an atomic-claim-level framework for evaluating the evidentiary reliability of LLM-generated Android forensic reports, testing Gemini, Llama, and Qwen across a public dataset case and a physical-device case.
motivation: Fluent LLM output does not guarantee evidentiary reliability in forensic reporting, so there is a need for auditable methods that verify claim support and citation validity rather than mere fluency or fact recall.
method: Six accepted LLM reports were decomposed into 612 claims and evaluated against frozen, human-reviewed authorities using content labeling, citation validation, fact-recall analysis, independent rechecking, and dispute resolution.
result: Of the 612 claims, 424 were supported and 163 unsupported (plus 4 contradicted, 4 overstated/incomplete, 17 excluded); citation validity varied wildly across models (Gemini 168/189, Qwen 145/189, Llama 0/135), and in the zero-reportable-fact physical-device case the models still produced 65 claims including 38 unsupported and 1 contradicted.
conclusion: Evidence restriction and complete fact recall do not guarantee claim-level support or valid evidence attribution, so investigator authority and auditable claim-to-evidence lineage must be retained over final forensic reports.

title: Adversarial Benchmarks And BenchDoor Attacks: Exploiting Benchmark Incentives For Backdoor Attacks
authors: Yixin Wu, Rachel Hong, Jamie Morgenstern, Tadayoshi Kohno
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning benchmarks act as guideposts for model development and spur the creation of training datasets intended to improve benchmark scores. We introduce BenchDoor, a family of data poisoning attacks that exploits this incentive. Beyond preserving benign performance, BenchDoor requires benchmark gains that encourage adoption of data that also implants a backdoor. The adversary either manipulates a benchmark's training or test data, creating an adversarial benchmark, or supplies an independent training dataset while leaving the benchmark unchanged. We formalize five attack scenarios, including training on rewritten test examples and applying similarity-based decontamination. Across multiple-choice Q&A, text classification, and open-ended Q&A with Qwen and Gemma models, BenchDoor achieves positive benchmark gains for all 30 evaluated configurations, with held-out attack success rates of 82.33% to 100.00% at poisoning rates of 2% to 10%. Both objectives remain achievable after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination, with attack success rates of at least 90.33%. These findings show how benchmarks can serve as attack vectors both through their own data and through training resources that deliver improvements on them.
tldr: The paper introduces BenchDoor, a family of data poisoning attacks that exploit benchmark incentives to implant backdoors while improving benchmark scores.
motivation: Machine learning benchmarks drive dataset creation and model development, creating incentives that adversaries can exploit to poison training or test data.
method: The authors formalize five attack scenarios involving manipulation of benchmark training/test data or independent training datasets, and evaluate them on multiple-choice QA, text classification, and open-ended QA with Qwen and Gemma models.
result: BenchDoor achieves positive benchmark gains in all 30 configurations and held-out attack success rates of 82.33%–100% at 2%–10% poisoning rates, remaining effective after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination with at least 90.33% attack success.
conclusion: Benchmarks can serve as attack vectors both through their own data and through training resources that appear to improve benchmark performance.

title: FoundPDE: A Generative Foundation Model For Data-driven Symbolic Discovery Of Partial Differential Equations
authors: Langchen Liu, Junlin Luo, Min Zhu, Zhuoran Yang, Lu Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from observed data is a central inverse problem in computational science and engineering: the goal is not only to predict trajectories, but to identify interpretable symbolic laws that can be analyzed and reused. Existing PDE discovery methods often depend on hand-designed libraries, accurate numerical derivatives, or per-equation symbolic search, making them fragile under sparse observations, noisy data, broad equation families, and unseen symbolic compositions. Here, we introduce FoundPDE, a pretrained data-to-symbol foundation model for PDE discovery. FoundPDE maps discretized spatio-temporal trajectories to symbolic equations with a transformer, uses Fourier and first-order spatial-derivative augmentation to expose complementary trajectory information, refines numerical coefficients, and supports downstream extension with improved generalization through few-shot fine-tuning and hierarchical discovery. On a clean in-domain benchmark spanning 20 PDE families, our model reaches 97.50% type recognition. Under coefficient shifts beyond the training support, type recognition remains 90.53%; under multiplicative Gaussian noise on the model input, it is 94.43% at a 2% noise level but falls to 52.09% at 10%. For unseen composite equations, few-shot fine-tuning reaches over 90% exact recovery on four held-out families, and we further develop a hierarchical discovery algorithm that recovers two-term composites without fine-tuning FoundPDE. By amortizing symbolic discovery across equation families, FoundPDE shifts PDE discovery from per-dataset search toward a reusable pretrained model that extends to new physics with limited additional data, a step toward foundation models that uncover interpretable governing laws directly from scientific data.
tldr: FoundPDE is a pretrained transformer-based foundation model that maps discretized spatio-temporal trajectory data directly to interpretable symbolic PDEs, amortizing symbolic discovery across equation families.
motivation: Existing PDE discovery methods rely on hand-crafted libraries, accurate numerical derivatives, and per-equation symbolic search, which are brittle under noise, sparse data, and unseen equation compositions.
method: The authors pretrain a transformer on data-to-symbol mappings augmented with Fourier and first-order spatial-derivative features, refine numerical coefficients post hoc, and support few-shot fine-tuning plus a hierarchical discovery algorithm for composite equations.
result: The model achieves 97.50% PDE type recognition on a 20-family in-domain benchmark, retains 90.53% under coefficient shifts and 94.43% at 2% input noise (dropping to 52.09% at 10%), and exceeds 90% exact recovery on four held-out composite families with few-shot fine-tuning.
conclusion: Amortizing symbolic PDE discovery into a reusable pretrained model shifts the paradigm from per-dataset search toward foundation models that uncover governing laws from scientific data with limited additional data.

title: Punctuated Equilibrium In Technological Capabilities: Commercial Selection And The Predictability Of Frontier Advances
authors: Dawoon Jeong Kenzi M'hamdi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolutionary accounts of technological change connect new technical opportunities with economic selection. Using approximately 1.74 million electronic-component product records, we examine the tempo of capability-frontier improvement alongside the diversity of commercially offered products. In a detailed analysis of 29 manually selected capabilities, 77.8% of substantial-advance episodes consist of a single observed advance year. Across eligible three-year windows beginning with an advance, the initial observed gain accounts for an average of 79.3% of total log-capability improvement. The median share of product records near the frontier is 1.46%. Motivated by the interaction of technology push and demand pull, we extend the analysis to 204 capabilities and conduct forward out-of-sample comparisons between models using frontier history and models additionally incorporating product composition, manufacturer competition, and population dynamics. The additional indicators do not improve forecasts of subsequent frontier advances. The results document concentrated frontier gains alongside a broad distribution of commercially offered specifications. Stylized comparisons of incremental service value and switching costs identify candidate mechanisms linking application-specific valuation and production scale to the economic relevance of technical opportunities. They also specify the price, quantity, and application-level observations needed to evaluate these interpretations. We propose source-grounded, language-model-assisted extraction of demand-related information from dated external documents, with validation against independently observed market data.
tldr: An empirical study of punctuated equilibrium in technological capability frontiers using 1.74 million electronic-component product records, showing frontier advances are concentrated in single-year jumps while commercial product specifications remain broadly distributed.
motivation: Evolutionary theories of technological change link new technical opportunities ('technology push') with economic selection ('demand pull'), but the empirical relationship between frontier improvement tempo and commercial product diversity is poorly quantified.
method: Analysis of ~1.74 million electronic-component product records across 29 manually curated and then 204 capabilities, measuring advance episodes, log-capability gains, and frontier-adjacent product shares, followed by out-of-sample forecasting comparisons with and without product-composition, competition, and population indicators.
result: 77.8% of substantial-advance episodes occur in a single observed year, the initial gain accounts for 79.3% of three-year improvement, and only a median 1.46% of products sit near the frontier; adding commercial indicators does not improve forecasts of subsequent frontier advances.
conclusion: Frontier technical gains are highly concentrated while commercial offerings are broad; the authors propose stylized mechanisms based on incremental service value and switching costs, and outline data needs plus LLM-assisted extraction of demand information to test them.

title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation Of Phase Equilibria For Transcritical Multiphase Flows
authors: Navneeth Srinivasan, Po-Yu Lai, Suo Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.26984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.
tldr: The paper develops an ISAT-ANN framework with load balancing and AMR for efficient phase-equilibrium tabulation in transcritical multiphase flow simulations.
motivation: High-pressure transcritical flow simulations with phase change are bottlenecked by costly and fragile vapor-liquid equilibrium calculations, while standalone neural networks and existing dynamic tabulation methods have efficiency and robustness limitations.
method: The authors combine in-situ adaptive tabulation with a pretrained ANN to replace iterative solvers during table expansion, add an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm for parallel efficiency, and couple the framework with adaptive mesh refinement.
result: On a Mach 5 shock-droplet benchmark, the framework captures shock-interface dynamics stably and achieves 2.30x single-core speedup, 2.62x parallel speedup over standalone ANNs, and an additional 2.92x overall efficiency boost from AMR.
conclusion: The plug-and-play ISAT-ANN framework provides a stable and scalable approach for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations, but it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Continuous And Differentiable Neural Network Representations Of The Surfzone Sea-Surface From Lidar Point Clouds
authors: David R. Culver, Matthias Morzfeld, Falk Feddersen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ocean waves are often analyzed via sea-surface observations. Multi-beam scanning lidar enables two-dimensional measurements of the water surface [MATH] via sequenced point clouds of sea-surface elevation. Point cloud data, however, have to be gridded, interpolated, or mapped for use in wave analysis. We present and test a method for creating a continuous and differentiable (space and time), but grid-free, representation of the sea-surface from time sequenced lidar point clouds. We use a specific neural network architecture, a SIREN, to represent the sea-surface and to train the network on spatiotemporal 60~s of lidar data collected by a gas-electric UAS (drone) hovering over large (4 m), breaking waves in Monterey, California. The trained SIREN allows estimation of the sea-surface and its derivatives at any location and time. SIREN sea-surface representations tend to filter the highest wave number variability (splash-up and sea-spray). SIREN errors are comparable to instrument errors and insensitive to local data density. The reliability and reproducibility of our approach is tested by training two SIRENs independently on the same data. Differences between the two independent SIRENs are comparable to instrument error, but increase in data-poor regions. SIRENs' potential for directional wave analysis is demonstrated by computing spatial and temporal derivatives and by estimating wave velocity from a SIREN-generated space-time slice of the sea-surface.
tldr: The paper uses SIREN implicit neural representations to build continuous, differentiable, grid-free models of the ocean surface from drone-mounted scanning lidar point clouds over breaking waves.
motivation: Lidar point clouds of the sea surface must be gridded or interpolated before wave analysis, which introduces artifacts and limits derivative-based analysis; a continuous, grid-free representation would avoid these issues.
method: A SIREN (sinusoidal activation) network is trained on ~60 s of spatiotemporal lidar point-cloud data collected by a hovering gas-electric UAS over 4 m breaking waves in Monterey, California, with error and reproducibility assessed via independent duplicate training runs.
result: SIREN errors are comparable to instrument error, insensitive to local point density, and tend to filter high-wavenumber splash/spray variability; discrepancies between independently trained networks are near instrument error but grow in data-sparse regions.
conclusion: Implicit neural representations offer a practical, differentiable sea-surface model enabling derivative-based and directional wave analysis, though reliability degrades where data are sparse.

title: On Diophantine Tuples Involving Star Numbers
authors: Sagar Mandal Tapas Chatterjee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we discuss two related Diophantine tuple problems involving star numbers [MATH]. First, we investigate classical [MATH]-tuples whose elements are star numbers. We construct infinitely many [MATH]-pairs for several positive and negative admissible values of [MATH], and we prove several nonexistence results for [MATH]-triples and quadruples. Second, we introduce a modified notion of a star number [MATH]-tuple, requiring [MATH] itself to be a star number. We construct several infinite families of [MATH]-triples, and study their extensions to quadruples. In particular, we prove that [MATH] has the unique extension [MATH] to a star number [MATH]-quadruple. The main tools used in this paper are generalized Pell equations, Nagell's theorem, lower bounds for linear forms in logarithms due to Matveev and Dujella-Peth version of the Baker-Davenport reduction method in diophantine approximation.
tldr: The paper studies Diophantine tuples whose elements are star numbers, constructing infinite families of D(n)-pairs and D(n)-triples and proving nonexistence and uniqueness results.
motivation: Classical Diophantine m-tuples (sets where pairwise products plus n are perfect squares) are a long-studied problem in number theory, and the authors extend this line of inquiry to the specific sequence of star numbers.
method: The proofs rely on generalized Pell equations, Nagell's theorem, Matveev's lower bounds for linear forms in logarithms, and the Baker-Davenport reduction method in the Dujella-Peth version.
result: Infinitely many D(n)-pairs are constructed for several admissible n, nonexistence of certain triples and quadruples is shown, and the triple involving star numbers is proved to have the unique extension to a star-number D(n)-quadruple.
conclusion: The work enriches the theory of Diophantine tuples by introducing star-number-constrained variants, though it remains purely within elementary/algebraic number theory.

title: Connected $\omega$-limit Sets Of Cournot Maps: Periodic Orbits, Realization And Almost Every Point
authors: Juan Luis Garc\'ia Guirao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a Cournot map of the unit square, [MATH] and [MATH]. Linero Bas and Mu\~noz Guillermo proved that an [MATH]-limit set of [MATH] with nonempty interior is connected if and only if its two projections are connected and [MATH], and conjectured that this holds for every [MATH]-limit set. We prove the conjecture for every point [MATH] such that [MATH] or [MATH] is finite, and for Lebesgue almost every point [MATH] of the square whenever [MATH] is metrically regular (every metric attractor is a periodic orbit, a solenoid, or a cycle of intervals carrying a well-behaved absolutely continuous invariant measure). Over a periodic orbit the [MATH]-limit set is a , whose sections are rigid; when one projection is connected it is a point, a [MATH] with [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH], or an of [MATH] disjoint segments. Conversely, every lattice and every alternating comb is an [MATH]-limit set of a Cournot map with piecewise linear reaction functions; the construction rests on a lemma producing exact compositions of piecewise linear maps with prescribed values. This answers, for this class, the question of Balibrea, Linero and C\'anovas of which nowhere dense sets are [MATH]-limit sets of Cournot maps. For instance, the letter H is not an [MATH]-limit set at any such point, and for metrically regular [MATH] the points whose [MATH]-limit set is connected, infinite, nowhere dense and not a lattice form a Lebesgue null set.
tldr: The paper proves a conjecture on connectedness of ω-limit sets of Cournot maps on the unit square, characterizing lattices and alternating combs and showing realizability by piecewise linear reaction functions.
motivation: Linero Bas and Muñoz Guillermo conjectured that an ω-limit set of a Cournot map with nonempty interior is connected iff its two projections are connected; this work aims to resolve the conjecture broadly and to classify which nowhere dense sets arise as ω-limit sets.
method: The authors establish the conjecture for points with a finite coordinate or for Lebesgue-almost every point when the map is metrically regular, and they construct Cournot maps with piecewise linear reaction functions using a lemma on exact compositions of piecewise linear maps.
result: Over periodic orbits the ω-limit set is a rigid lattice-like structure; when a projection is connected it is a point, a segment family, or a union of disjoint segments, and every lattice and alternating comb is realized as an ω-limit set.
conclusion: The work answers a classification question of Balibrea, Linero and Cànovas for this class of maps, showing e.g. that the letter H is never such an ω-limit set and that certain connected, infinite, nowhere dense non-lattice limit sets form a Lebesgue null set.

title: Counting Who Counts: Black Women Mathematicians In The United States
authors: Olayemi Adeyemi, Ron Buckmire, Ranthony A. Clark, Shanzhen Gao, Jakini Kauba, Lakeshia Legette-Jones, Apoorva Mate, Omayra Ortega, Jos\'e Pab\'on, Robin T. Wilson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.27395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For Black women in the mathematical sciences, histories have frequently been fragmented or omitted from official records, an absence that itself constitutes a form of exclusion. This project addresses this critical gap by constructing a curated dataset of 147 Black women who have earned doctoral degrees in mathematics and related mathematical sciences in the United States. By integrating archival research, institutional records, digital databases, and community knowledge, we establish a reproducible methodology for identifying, verifying, and documenting Black women mathematicians. We situate this dataset within a broader history of efforts to document Black mathematicians and describe how prior archival and community based initiatives informed its development.
